speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
I should like to say just a word about the Geneva agreement, which has been before the house for consideration. Hon. members will recall that some time ago I introduced a motion respecting this agreement. The motion appears as item No. 3 under government orders:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve the general agreement on tariffs and trade, including the protocol of provisional application thereof . . .
In the course of the debate the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) moved an amendment with a view to separating the part of the resolution which referred to the British preference from the rest of the motion so that there would be two resolutions instead of one, in order that these matters could be debated separately. The idea was that the part relating to the Geneva agreement would go to a committee. I indicated at the time that the government would be prepared to facilitate the agreement going before a committee.
The matter has been gone into carefully and there has been some conference with hon. gentlemen opposite who lead the different parties. As a result of what has been considered it seems that the best means to bring about what is desired would be to have an amendment moved to the amendment which
the hon. member for Vancouver South has moved to the original motion. The amendment would have as its purpose to divide the original resolution into two parts and have them appear on the order paper as two separate resolutions. This is a matter of procedure.
Perhaps the best course would be for me to leave the matter at the moment as I have explained it and to say that tomorrow, if the house is agreeable, I shall ask that we proceed to divide the original resolution in the manner I have directed. In order to do that I will ask one of my colleagues to move an amendment to the amendment of my hon. friend in the following words:
That the amendment be amended-
(a)	by deleting the words "referred to the committee of the whole house with instruction to divide" and substituting therefor the words "divided as to"; and
(b)	by adding at the end of the said amendment the following:
"the said resolutions to be expressed as follows:-"
The first resolution would read:
That is is expedient that parliament do approve the general agreement on tariffs and trade, including the protocol of provisional application thereof, annexed to the final act of the second session of the preparatory committee of the united nations conference on trade and employment held at Geneva from April 10 to October 30, 1947, together with the complementary agreement of October 30, 1947, between Canada and the United States of America; that the house do approve the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof;
The second resolution would read:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve the complementary agreement of October 30, 1947, between Canada and the United Kingdom relating to the general agreement on tariffs and trade, and that the house do approve the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.
I give this as a notice at the moment. If hon. members would look carefully at what I have said between now and tomorrow, if it is then agreeable to the house we could proceed tomorrow with the suggested amendment to the amendment. This would facilitate having the Geneva agreement referred forthwith to a committee. The government would be glad to facilitate that procedure and would wish to take it. I might say that I understand
Tariffs and Trade

the committee to which hon. gentlemen opposite would wish to have the Geneva agreement referred is not a special committee of the house or a joint committee of the two houses; it is the standing committee on banking and commerce. That would be quite agreeable to the government if that is what is desired.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved:
That a select committee be appointed to consider the legislation relating to pensions, treatment and re-establishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces and of other persons who have been otherwise engaged in pursuits closely related to war, and to make recommendations from time to time in respect thereto.
That the committee shall have power to send for persons, papers and records, and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee.
That the committee shall have leave to sit while the house is sitting.
That eighteen members of the committee shall constitute a quorum.
That the committee shall consist of Messrs. Baker, Belzile, Benidickson. Bentley, Blair, Blanchette, Brooks, Croll, Cruickshank, Dickey, Dion. Emmerson, Gauthier (Portneuf), Gregg, Green, Harris (Grey-Bruee), Harkness, Her-rid'ge, Isnor, Jutras, Langlois, Leonard, Mac-Naught, McKay, Marshall, Moore, Mutch, Pearkes, Quelch, Ross (Souris), Skey, Tucker, Viau, White (Hastings-Peterborough), Wright, and that paragraph li of standing order 65 be suspended in relation thereto.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in presenting this
resolution it is not my purpose to enter into a full report of the work of my department since last year. I shall be very glad to submit all matters affecting that work to this committee and at appropriate times to the house. By setting aside today to discuss this resolution the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has already indicated the desire of the government to have this committee set up, and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I shall
*953

Veterans Affairs Committee
not kill the hope I have that it may be set up today by entering into a long discussion at this stage.
First I should like to say a word about the former parliamentary committees dealing with veterans matters. During the twenty years between the great wars a good deal of ground was broken relating to questions arising out of the old war. Some hon. members will recall that during the period when the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) was my predecessor in this department certain advances were made, but even so, when the committee appointed during and immediately after this last war came into being, hon. members who sat on the committee were faced with a, task of great importance. The new situation introduced many new features, and I think, Mr. Speaker, a word of tribute might well be paid to those committees for the way in which they approached those problems, for the evidence they sifted and the non-partisan manner in which they went at their task, and lastly that they were able to bring in the foundation for a comprehensive program for the veterans.
I think it was important that that program was comprehensive from the very start and did not come in piecemeal after demobilization had begun. It was also important that it was ready in good time, and for that result the committee which sat during the war deserves credit. Being ready in good time, the information arising out of the committee s report and the legislation of this house, in liaison with the Department of National Defence, was carried to service people in all parts of the world, and in that way a receptive spirit was built up before service personnel came out of uniform. When they did come back, as soon as their demobilization was completed the plans were there ready for them to enter into.
There is another fact worth mentioning, and that is the relation of the work of the committee to the whole Canadian population. At the end of this war the people as a whole throughout Canada were determined that this time nothing should be left undone to make rehabilitation and re-establishment work. A good many old veterans of the first world war looked with a good deal of concern on their past experience and wondered whether the fervour at the end of this war would have as short a life and become swallowed up in materialism as it was in the early twenties. The work of the committee carried forward to parliament and interpreted to the people in Canada did much to crystallize that desire on the part of the Canadian people, and1 I am
glad to say that that co-operation on their part has been sustained down to the present time.
I should like also to pay tribute to the happy relations that existed between these committees, during the war and after, and my department. The department, under the vigorous and able leadership of my predecessor, had a terrific task with which to cope. Hon. members will recall that in 1945 the tempo of demobilization was greatly accelerated when compared with that which was anticipated. This afternoon we are proposing a new committee. In that committee there will be the opportunity to find out how this plan has been working. I am free to state that as minister I shall welcome any well-conceived and constructive suggestions on how to improve on the plan administratively.
The committee may also want to hear and consider representations regarding the plan from persons and bodies in various parts of Canada.
May I say a word or two on points of detail. Following the resolution a bill will be introduced reflecting the announced increase in pensions. The government will be very glad to have that bill pass through all stages as early as possible. Whether all hon. members agree with all the details of the bill as forecast, I am sure that that would be their wish. I have looked into the' matter, and if it is possible for this bill to pass through all its stages in a short time it will be possible administratively for the approximately 200,000 files to be checked and brought up to date for the mechanism to be carried out to convert them into cheques and for those cheques to be received by veterans in the early part of April, if authority can be given by Easter. If we could obtain unanimous consent I would be prepared to recommend the approval of the bill this afternoon, and then submit it to the committee on veterans affairs for study or adopt any other procedure to make it possible. The other legislation forecast will move forward without delay. So far as the increases in the allowances to the dependents of student veterans in training is concerned I should like to state that these increases will be reflected in the cheques going out at the end of this month.
I am quite certain that this committee will approach its task with earnestness of purpose and energy, and I commend it to the favourable consideration of this house.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PENSIONS, TREATMENT AND RE-ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first offer my congratulations to the minister on his maiden speech on veterans affairs. We have now been sitting foT three
Veterans Affairs Committee

months. We had hoped, of course, that this very important matter would have been before the house long ago. I am glad that we are now taking steps to see that the veterans of this country receive in some measure the rights to which they are entitled. I do regret, as I know other hon members in this house have regretted, the long time it has taken to set up this committee. When the house met last December it was recommended by myself, and by many other hon. members on this side of the house, that a veterans committee be immediately set up. We are anxious that the veterans of this country should receive the benefits to which they are entitled and which we all know they need.
I mentioned some few weeks ago that the great rise in the cost of living had imposed many hardships on the veterans, and as I said a moment ago, we had hoped that a veterans committee would be set up and that these bills would be passed through the house and that the veterans would have received this relief which I know they are all waiting for.
The minister has said that it is his intention to submit all matters of the department to the veterans committee. That is as it should be. The veterans committee has worked on veterans affairs for a great many years. I join with the minister in congratulating the committees which have worked in the past. His tribute to them today is well merited. He said there had been happy relations between the different parties. As a member of a number of veterans committees I can state with a clear conscience that so far as I am concerned there have been very happy relations between the different parties that worked on the different veterans committees.
The minister also mentioned a bill having to do with increases in pensions and said that he hoped it would be passed as quickly as possible.
I would point out to him that his hurry now does not seem altogether in keeping with the actions which the government has taken during the past three months. Today, after three months of delay, the minister tells us that they are very anxious to rush through legislation. I would point out to him and to the government that this could have been done, and should have been done, many weeks ago. The minister has also emphasized the great change in veterans legislation. Year after year we note that veterans legislation is never finished. Something is always coming up; new situations arise which make it necessary to make changes in veterans legislation. I suggest now-it has been suggested by many hon. members on different occasions-that there should be a standing committee of the house on veterans affairs. If a standing committee had been 
appointed last year when it was suggested, we would not be waiting until almost the middle of March, although the house met in December, to deal with veterans affairs. Instead of receiving these cheques, which the minister mentioned, in April, they would be receiving them now. I do impress upon the minister and upon the house the great necessity of setting up a standing committee on veterans affairs.
The minister reviewed somewhat the history of veterans committees. We all remember that the first committee was set up in 1916, I think. This committee started from scratch. They had no precedent to follow so far as their work was concerned, but we all agree that they did splendid work. Many committees have been set up since. That is another point which bears out my argument that we should have a standing committee. Since the first committee was set up in 1916 to the outbreak of this war there have been sixteen committees. There have been four committees since, making some twenty in all, which only emphasizes the fact that a standing committee is a necessary committee in this necessary work.
I need only mention the names of the men who headed the first committee to show the prominence that has been given to veterans affairs. We had such men as the Hon. W. F. Nickle, the Hon. Newton Wesley Rowell, Hon. Hume Cronyn, the Hon. Sir Herbert Marler, the Hon. Cyrus Macmillan, the Hon. C. G. Power, and last, but not least,
I am sure, the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker), the present leader of the opposition in Saskatchewan and who, I am sure, will attain to that honourable position of leader of His Majesty's loyal opposition in that province after the next election.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PENSIONS, TREATMENT AND RE-ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
If such a committee had been set up it would not have been necessary to go through all this red tape in setting it up at the present time. Had it been set up last year it would have been operating before Christmas and pensioners would now have had their increase, war veterans would have had their increase in allowance, and many other benefits would already have been received by veterans.
This committee is smaller than the committee we had in 1945 and 1946. I feel that

Veterans Affairs Committee
in setting up a committee again the men who worked so hard in those years to prepare the so-called veterans charter should have been the same men on the committee at this time. I feel that the house and the committee are losing the valuable experience of many men who are very well versed in veterans affairs and who are extremely anxious to help in this work.
I know that these men were very anxious to be on the committee. As far as the terms of reference are concerned, the minister said a moment ago that all matters pertaining to veterans would be referred to the committee. The resolution reads:
That a select committee be appointed to consider the legislation relating to pensions, treatment and re-establishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces and of other persons who have been otherwise engaged in pursuits closely related to war, and to make recommendations from time to time in respect thereto.
I would call the minister's attention to the fact that, besides making recommendations, the resolution in 1945 gave the committee the opportunity and the right to submit draft bills to the house, and I am wondering why that was left out of the present resolution.
Another matter which I think deserves our attention is the fact that in mentioning the armed forces the merchant marine has not been included as such. We on this side of the house have advocated time and again, and we have argued, that men of the merchant marine should be included in the armed forces. Men of the merchant marine were told during the last war, by men of high standing in the government, that they were the fourth arm as far as service is concerned. It is not necessary for me to enlarge upon that; the facts are too well known to the house. We do feel, however, that the merchant marine, the men of the merchant navy, have not received and are not today receiving the justice they are entitled to from this Canadian house of parliament.
Having this in view, I should like to offer an amendment to the resolution, as follows, moved by myself and seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South:
That the motion be amended by inserting, after the word "forces" in the third line thereof, the following, "including the merchant navy."
The resolution will then read:
That a select committee be appointed to consider the legislation relating to pensions, treatment and re-establishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces, including the merchant navy, and of other persons who have been otherwise engaged in pursuits closely related to war, and to make recommendations from time to time in respect thereto.
And so on.
Like the minister I do not intend this afternoon to go into all phases of veterans affairs, but there are a few matters I should like to refer to. We often hear a comparison made in this house with other nations, and we are told, when we ask for benefits for our men, that our veterans legislation is the best in the world. That is a very general statement, Mr. Speaker, and one which I do not think will always bear very close scrutiny. I am not saying that our veterans legislation is not good. It is good. But in some points we feel it could be improved, and I do not agree, as has been stated, that the veterans legislation in Canada is, on balance, the best legislation in the world. I took the trouble not long ago to write to Washington to get reports on veterans legislation in that country, and I was amazed at some of the benefits which the veterans of the United States receive in comparison with our Canadian veterans.
I will not take time this afternoon to give a detailed list, but among some of those benefits I would mention that the student who goes to a university receives free textbooks, which is a great benefit to the man attending university. That is besides free tuition, which we of course give in Canada. The veteran there also receives one extra year besides the time of service. Here in Canada our veterans receive 860 a month for every month they served in the army. In the United States they receive $75 a month, but they not only receive that for the time they served in the army; they also receive a year's bonus. That is, if a man served in the army 18 months he would get 30 months' tuition at the university at the rate of pay I have mentioned. Again, the veteran who is disabled, who has lost a leg or an arm, is given a free car up to $1,600 a year. A man who is blind has provision made for him. He is given a seeing-eye dog. There are other advantages which I think the blind man should have. There is also a helplessness allowance. In Canada our men receive $750 a year. The Americans pay up to $360 a month for helpless pensioners. I might also say that, going over this list, besides what is received from the central government in the United States, every state in the American union has passed laws granting benefits to their returned men. When this is all considered, when it is all added up, it is not a fact to say that Canadian legislation provides more than any other country in the world.
I should like to mention another matter which appeals to me very strongly and that is the question of preference in employment. I am not going to discuss civil service employment; so far as the civil service is concerned, taking it in general, with some exceptions of
Veterans Affairs Committee

course, the civil service preference has been fairly well carried out. But there are many other preferences in employment besides those under the civil service.
From the very highest to the lowest in this country, there are positions which do not come under the civil service. I would mention, for instance, the matter of appointments to senatorships and judgeships. After the last war, as we all know, men, who were very prominent in the war were appointed to the senate irrespective of political affiliations. The same applied to judgeships. Taking my own province as an example, I know that during the last three or four years, in appointments, as far as judgeships and senatorships are concerned, the veterans preference has never been taken into consideration. At the present time we have a situation in the province of New Brunswick to which I should like to call attention. Chief Justice Baxter, who was one of the most learned jurists, I suppose, in the dominion, passed away nearly a year ago. Mr. Justice Harrison, who has since been acting as chief justice, is a judge of very high standing; I suppose few judges in Canada have a higher standing than he has. He was a veteran of the first world war, but he has not been appointed chief justice. Mr. Justice Harrison would make a splendid chief justice, but because he did not belong to the right political party we have to wait for the time to come when a political appointment can be made. I say that these things are not right. It is the duty of the federal government to set an example in matters of this kind. We complain of discrimination in some of the lower appointments, but if there is discrimination in the higher appointments we cannot very well complain of it when we meet it in some of the minor appointments.
There is a matter to which I wish to refer, Mr. Speaker, and it is something that has been called to my attention on numerous occasions. I have received a number of letters about it and have been asked to place it before the House of Commons. It has to do with this question of political discrimination.
I quote from the Halifax Mail of Wednesday, November 19, 1947. The heading of this article is "Political discrimination against vets charged", and it reads as follows:
Discrimination against war veterans in flavour of political workers was condemned at a meeting of the executive council of the provincial command, Canadian Legion, during an all-day session at Halifax on Monday. Following heated discussion which arose over a letteT by a Halifax county Liberal party chairman, the executive committee released a statement and the [DOT]text of the letter, with a request that both be published.

I might point out that the executive council of the provincial command, Canadian, Legion, in Nova Scotia-as in every other part of this dominion-is a non-political organization. These men are not politicians. They belong to all parties. The membership is made up of members of every party there is in this country. The only object they have is to see that the veterans get what they consider a square deal. The article continues:
The Legion's statement with the names omitted from the letter quoted is published herewith. Canadian Legion, officers said they have the names on file.
"There was a heated discussion in the meeting of the executive council of the Nova Scotia command of the Canadian Legion over apparent discrimination against war veterans in favour of political workers in Nova Scotia government projects. Particular indignation was voiced against an attitude which was considered all too prevalent"-
I should like to emphasize those words, "against an attitude which was considered all too prevalent."
-expressed in a letter which frankly stated that a war veteran to hold a government job must vote for the Liberal party. The full text of this letter from the chairman of a patronage committee to the secretary of a Canadian Legion branch, follows.
If I may comment on that expression "all too prevalent", this indicates that it is not an isolated case. If it were, I would say nothing about it. But where one man has the temerity and is stupid and foolish enough to put his thoughts on paper, there are hundreds of cases in which the facts are not published. I might say in this connection that I know of many similar cases in my own province of New Brunswick. I will not read all of the letter. The chairman sets out what his position is, then he goes on to say:
From the general theme of your letter-
That is the letter he received from the chairman of the provincial command of the Canadian Legion in that district.
-one would gather that only a veteran need be protected in this land of ours. What about the men on the home front who made it possible before, during and now since the war is over, for such people as the veteran to be taken cate of?
That shows the mental attitude of this man. To continue:
One would think some political scheme was being endorsed an, laying Mr. Blank-
I have the name here.
-off the road now under construction. Since you speak a great deal of the Liberal committee, Mr. Blank, being a veteran and not being asked his political views when enlisting; well, I think if you probe a little deeper into the

Veterans Affairs Committee
matter you'll find that when he went to enlist for a job on the road he wasn't asked that particular question either, but we did' think, and I think you'll quite readily agree also, that after being employed since early spring under a Liberal government project, plus having the polling station on his premises on election dtay, he would cast a vote in our favour. Now if that isn't protecting the veteran, I do not know what other terms it could come under, to give a man such a chance as this, then in return only ask the marking of an insignificant little "x" for John Dickey when election day came. But no, he would not consider,, and it is perfectly right that the truck that filled the gap was a non-veteran, but not a non-worker for the Liberal government.
That is the attitude, Mr. Speaker, of this particular man. He goes on to say:
May I acquaint you with the fact that these orders were from under the same jurisdiction that passed the legislation for Legion protection. We do absolutely nothing on our own.
He does not say he is doing it on his own. He says it is done by the orders of the same people who passed the legislation for Legion protection. They do it on the suggestion of someone else. He goes to say:
They are back of us 100 per cent all the way. In other words the Liberal government is running this affair and not the Canadian Legion, so if you want to take steps in any way, take them to further co-opeTation of the servicemen, for some of them want all in all. I consider they are being greatly taken care of, so much so that they should support us when election time comes if they had to crawl on hand and knee to the polling booth to cast a Liberal vote.

speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PENSIONS, TREATMENT AND RE-ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not think we ever heard) such a political philosophy as that, to the effect that the veteran, the working man, besides giving an honest day's work for an honest day's pay which he receives from public money paid1 to the government by all parties in this country, must give his vote to the government party. Surely the working man is entitled to his share whether he votes for the Liberal party or whether he votes for some other party. To ask that he sacrifice his rights as a citizen of this country, and to give up his right to vote as he pleases-a right won for him by great sacrifices over a long period of time-is to me, Mr. Speaker, a philosophy of nazism, a philosophy which these men fought to destroy in Europe; it is a philosophy which is eating at the very heart of this world today in connection with communism.
This, as I say, was not even an isolated1 case in that particular district, because the writer of this letter goes on to say:
I may say in passing that we dealt with a case similar to this already this summer, when
a so-called veteran boasted very highly of putting his truck on the road without consulting me. He told Mr. Blank as much as that in my presence, but right then and there Mr. Blank brought the lad down to earth and forced him to eat humble pie or else.
There is more to this letter but I do not think I will take the time of the house to read further. I do believe this indicates the attitude of this particular man, and as I have said it is quite a general attitude in many parts of the maritime provinces at the present time. The article states:
The Legion is pressing for the principle followed by the federal government in granting a preference in employment in all government projects to war veterans. They cannot recognize as valid the principle that workers for a political party have a claim on the people of this province superior to that of the veteran who served his country in the hours of her greatest need.
Someone may ask why I bring this matter before the House of Commons. As I stated a short time ago, in the first place I brought it up here because it had been called to my attention by a great many people; and in the second place because I think it represents a very unjust principle which is being practised in many parts of this country. I had another reason for bringing it up here. A few weeks ago in moving for the appointment of a committee to inquire into price increases the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said publicity was the greatest weapon that could be used against any person guilty of meanness toward his fellow men. These were his words, to be found at page 747 of Hansard for February 2:
Whatever men may be in their individual lives, there is nothing they abhor more, if they have been guilty of any meanness or taken any undue advantage of their fellow men, than to have that meanness exposed in public.
That, was one of the more important reasons that impelled me to raise this matter today. The Prime Minister went on to say:
I for one firmly believe dn the power of publicity when based on facts. Public opinion plays a very large part in determining the course of events and the conduct of human beings.
I do not think it necessary to comment further on that point. I am not accusing the Premier of Nova Scotia of being guilty of this act. I do not think he is; but, we all know it is not always the men at the top who do the mean things as far as politics is concerned. Throughout the country we have men in smaller positions, chairmen of committees or men holding small jobs which they wish to protect. They are not so much interested, perhaps, in having the premier elected as in seeing that their own jobs are protected,

Veterans Affairs Committee
and they do everything possible to this end. I think it is more necessary now than ever before that we jealously preserve our democratic principles. It may be said that this has happened on other occasions. I can neither deny nor affirm that; but today we are living under conditions very different from those which obtained years ago. Today we have thousands of men employed by the government whereas years ago there were very few such jobs, in comparison. Today some say half our people are receiving cheques from the government. I do not know whether that is altogether true, but there is no doubt we have millions of people in receipt of benefits from the government. This being so, as I said a moment ago it is more important than ever before that in matters of this kind we exercise the greatest possible care. It is not good for a country that the party in power should be able to fortify themselves by these methods and perpetuate their tenure of office. I believe it calls for a greater fight on behalf of the plain citizen, the little man in the country district who pays his taxes, who is willing and anxious to work. He should be given the same protection, and should enjoy the same benefits from the taxes he and his friends pay, as the man who votes for a certain party. These job holders have become arrogant and arbitrary. They are the little dictators, the little tyrants of the political party in their own districts. As I said before, their main idea is to keep their government in power so they may protect their jobs. I should like to read what Musquodoboit harbour branch No. 82 of the Canadian Legion had to say about this letter:
The incredibly offensive tone of that letter is an almost unbelievable insult to every ex-service man. For an agent of a political party to make such a statement that veterans should be willing to crawl on their hands and knees to the polling booth to vote Liberal-presumably in gratitude for the benefits of D.V.A.-is a dangerous, tactless provocation of the cheapest kind . . .
If there is any point of gratitude involved in veterans' affairs it should surely be gratitude on the part of people like the patronage chairman that they are not now having the hide whipped off them in an SS concentration camp.
I have made inquiries, Mr. Speaker, and it would seem to me that this man in particular should have been dismissed. That is one of the things which should have been done immediately this was made public. My understanding is that it has not been done. An example should be made of this man and others guilty of such offences; that is the only way to clear up a situation which I

know is becoming more prevalent all the time, at least in the maritime provinces.
A few weeks ago I discussed veterans affairs in some detail. The minister says all such matters are to be sent to the committee, and as a member of that committee I will have an opportunity to discuss them there. Therefore I have no further remarks to make this afternoon.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PENSIONS, TREATMENT AND RE-ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire at this time to make a few observations with regard to the resolution to set up a select committee on veterans affairs. This committee is to consider legislation relating to pensions, treatment and re-establishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces and of other persons who have been otherwise engaged in pursuits closely related to war. That seems to me to be a very large order. There are in this country 800,000 veterans of the last world war. When one adds to that number the veterans of world war I and their dependents, as well as the dependents of the second world war veterans and all the groups related to the various pursuits that were close to war such as the merchant marine, the nursing services, the men who flew in ferry command and the fire fighters, the total of those we have to deal with assumes staggering proportions.
The Department of Veterans Affairs is one of the heavy departments dealing with national welfare, and it certainly is one of the most important. When the estimates of this department are brought before the house they are subjected to the closest scrutiny. They are frequently held up, however, by the discussion of special cases. These special cases have to be dealt with but I do not consider the floor of the house is the place to do it. These special cases, or perhaps they might be called marginal cases, have to be considered by some person or some group in authority. I suggest that in order to facilitate the passage of the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs a permanent parliamentary committee be set up. There is no doubt in my mind that weeks could be lopped off every parliamentary session if a permanent committee on veterans affairs was functioning throughout the session. There was no committee last session, and the passage of the estimates of this particular
Veterans Affairs Committee

department was slow and tedious, despite the fact that we had a minister who was genial and co-operative. I submit that in the best interests of the veterans at large and of the proper conduct of the work of this house it would be wise to set up a permanent parliamentary committee to deal1 with veterans problems.
There are a great many problems to be considered by the suggested committee. I shall refer to only a few of them because I do not want to be accused of holding up this resolution. I believe the whole schedule of pensions and the schedule of allowances referred to by the previous speaker should be revised. Pensions and allowances still remain at the basic rate which was struck in 1926. There have been a few adjustments made but they are totally inadequate and still insufficient to enable the veteran, and his family to enjoy the standard of living which the schedule of 1926 intended them to have. The present pensions are inadequate because of the increased cost of living and because today the Canadian standard of living is higher than it was twenty-two years ago.
I feel also that the single veteran student should have been included in the recent increases granted to recipients of training allowances. These young men and women are experiencing grave, difficulty in carrying on their courses because of financial need. They receive S60 a month, which seems a considerable figure to some of us who struggled through university on much less, but the cost of living in those days was nothing compared to what it is today. I suggest that because of the increase in the cost of living-it has gone up about twenty-five per cent since 1944-the training allowances schedule be revised upward. It seems only fair that the single veteran student should be included along with the married veteran in the change of schedule rates.
I would also wish that the committee be again allowed to consider the granting of clear title to the soldier settlers of 1919. There is still an average of over $1,000-SI,089, to be exact-against each farm unit after the passage of twenty-nine years. These men have struggled for years trying to make ends meet. Surely after twenty-nine years it is time to right this wrong and rectify an injustice. The interest rates were too high; this has been generally conceded, and care was not exercised in many cases in the choice of land. Others were the victims of circumstances. I hope this matter may be again discussed in the committee.

Another matter which deserves the serious consideration of the committee is the rehabilitation of Canada's merchant seamen, the fourth arm of the service, as they were frequently called. As far as I am aware there are no merchant seamen in my constituency, but I do feel that the merchant seamen have been the victims of an injustice. I feel that they should have received the same rehabilitation grants and more particularly the same training allowances, as veterans received. True, they were not in uniform, but they rendered an invaluable service to Canada in her hour of greatest danger. Their casualties were heavy, their sufferings great. These brave men should be given an opportunity to make representations to the committee. That same opportunity should be given to a few other groups I shall mention. I feel that we should ask for representations, for instance, from the men of the ferry command, the fire fighters, war amputations, and the nursing services.
Finally I think there ought to be an investigation into the failure of the Veterans Land Act. It has failed to provide farms for thousands of veterans who have been clamouring for land in the west. Settlement has been slow, too slow. Many have been unable to get established despite the fact land is available everywhere. The loan granted is inadequate. I said so two years ago in this house. It is even more true today. The administration of the act appears cumbersome and inefficient. A recent return made in this house gives us some interesting figures regarding the slowness of settlement and the cost of loans to veterans. These figures are taken from sessional paper 134E, 1948. It shows that only 846 veterans were settled under the Veterans Land Act in 1947 in the province of Saskatchewan. The total number settled since 1943 in Saskatchewan up until December 31, 1947, the end of the last calendar year, was only 4,029. That is an average of approximately 1,000 veterans settled per year. The number of veterans who desire land in Saskatchewan has been estimated at some 30,000. That estimate was arrived at by taking the number of veterans who had enlisted from Saskatchewan in this war and comparing it with the number of veterans who were settled under the old soldier settlement scheme of 1919. Settling our veterans on land at the rate of 1,000 per year is not fast enough. At this rate it will take from twenty-five to thirty years to do the job and accommodate the men who want land.
The expenses for administration under the Veterans Land Act also appear to be excessive. In Saskatchewan alone, according to this same sessional paper, there were paid under the

Veterans Affairs Committee
Veterans Land Act for travelling expenses, $39,009.40; salaries, $318,129.64; rent, local, $127; miscellaneous, $40,536.28. There was also a further amount paid by the Department of Public Works for rent, light, heat, taxes and so forth, the figures for which are not given in the return. The total expenses for 1947 for administration were $397,848.32 by the figures revealed. When one divides this cost by the 846 loans which were approved in the province of Saskatchewan in 1947 it works out at $470 per loan. Added to that of course must be the pro rata share of the extra expenses paid by other departments, mainly public works, for rent, light, heat and that sort of thing, for which no figures are given in the return. The total amount of money lent to veterans in Saskatchewan for 1947 was $3,588,790, or an average loan of $4,240. Therefore the cost of administration is more than eleven per cent, plus the extras previously referred to, which might run to another ten per cent.
This indicates an unsatisfactory state of affairs. The whole program under the Veterans Land Act ought to be thoroughly scrutinized and most carefully investigated.
It must be apparent to all, Mr. Speaker, certainly to all members of this house, that there is a great deal of work to be done by this select committee on veterans affairs. I feel it is a matter for some regret that the committee was not set up earlier. There are many important and urgent problems to be dealt with. It is my hope, however, that much can be done in the weeks ahead to assist the veteran in the solution of the many grave problems with which he is confronted today.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PENSIONS, TREATMENT AND RE-ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief because I am a member of the committee and shall have plenty of opportunity there to say what I think should be done. We in this group appreciate the work and the sincerity of the former minister of veterans affairs, and we are afraid that the present minister will in all probability run into the same obstacle his predecessor so often ran into, namely, adverse decisions of the treasury board.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Oregg) this afternoon gave us the assurance that the terms of reference of the committee would be wide enough to permit all matters relating to his department to come before the committee. After reading the terms of the reference I should have thought they were wide enough to permit a full discussion of the merchant navy without the moving of the amendment, because, as I remember it, the
merchant navy was not specifically mentioned in former terms of reference; nevertheless we did discuss the merchant navy in former committees.
It will be recalled that at the time the veterans charter was being considered by the special committee on veterans affairs in 1946, a great deal of dissatisfaction was expressed at the inadequacy of some of the measures contained therein. Subsequent events have proven that the dissatisfaction was justified at that time. Consequently the failure of the government to bring down certain amendments to veterans legislation has, in many cases, caused extreme hardship.
Having in mind that the Department of Veterans Affairs will be making heavy expenditures on behalf of veterans for a number of years and that veterans problems will continue to be acute ones in the future, we also think it would be a good idea if the government would make the committee on veterans affairs a standing one, so that from year to year the committee would be in a position to deal with various matters relating to veterans without having to wait for several years before a special committee was set up.
We in this group would like to join in the protest that has been made regarding the inadequacy of the government's proposal with reference to an increase in disability pensions. We do not believe that such a low rate can be justified, having in mind that the cost of living, apart from rent, has increased by 40 per cent since the rate of pensions was last set. We feel that the legion request for a 25 per cent increase for all beneficiaries under the Pension Act is a reasonable one. Then, the present procedure of reducing pensions of veterans of world war I when examination shows a reduction in their disability is an extremely vicious one. After all, it is approximately thirty years since the first war, and the average age of the veteran is now fifty-nine; yet the government apparently tries to save a few dollars by penalizing those old veterans, and the consequence of that has been some tragic incidents, incidents that we have all regretted. Since that time most people, I think, feel it would have been a good idea if the government had made the present rate of pensions for veterans of world war I the floor, and that any revision made in the future should be upwards only.
I should like to say a few words with respect to the War Veterans Allowance Act. Probably some of the most tragic cases of hardship may be found amongst recipients of the war veterans allowances. I want to make it clear, however, that I am not for one min-
Veterans Affairs Committee

ute criticizing the administration of the act. I believe that those responsible for the administration of the act have always gone out of their way to be as generous as the act permits. The whole trouble is that the amount payable under the act is altogether too low to meet the current cost of living, and this is further aggravated by the ceiling on additional income. We feel that the rates should be raised at least to the level of $50 a month, without any means test. I think the means test is the main curse of the War Veterans Allowance Act. Furthermore, the ceiling allowed is restricted by the regulations governing the method by which the additional income may be earned or acquired. An additional income of $400 a year is allowed, of which only $250 may be earned income, $125 casual earnings and $25 interest from investment. If there were no strings attached to the additional income, if the veteran were allowed $400, it would not be quite so bad. To have a ceiling of $400 for additional income is altogether too low. If the government is not prepared to remove the means test, at least it could allow the veteran to have an income up to the amount of the exemption from income tax, which would be $1,500 at the present time.
I should like to say a few words regarding student veterans. We have received many letters from student veterans with regard to the scale of allowances and the fact that many of them have had to discontinue their studies on account of lack of funds. I cannot understand how any veteran would have to give up his studies on account of lack of funds, having in mind the fact that in the committee we dealt with legislation to grant to student veterans loans of $2,000. Therefore, when I received a brief from the National Council of Student Veterans of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba on this question I wrote to them asking how it was that veterans were having to discontinue their studies. I asked them whether or not these veterans had made use of the loan, and I should like to quote one part of the letter which I received with reference to these loans. The writer says:
Regarding point (1) above, I agree with you that the terms of the loan are easy. The problem that many students have is in obtaining the loan. Apparently individual universities vary considerably in their conditions which determine eligibility for the loan. For example, a certain eastern university has discouraged the loan practice to such an extent that the students have lost hope of even attempting to obtain it. At the other extreme is a western varsity which can produce a long list of satisfied loan seekers. The students merely ask and they receive. I have had personal experience with the loan board of the University of

Saskatchewan. On this campus the loan is viewed as an emergency measure only, and money is not given out unless definite proof is presented in the form of doctor bills, promissory motes, etc.
This letter is signed by Donald French, representative of the National Council of Student Veterans. I was quite surprised to get this letter, because when we discussed this matter in committee we were given to understand that these loans would be made available to help any student who found he was not able to carry on his studies. We now find that definite limitations are being placed upon the use of the loans. Therefore I urge the minister to make a thorough investigation into the whole question of loans in the various universities throughout the country to find out just what restrictions are being imposed upon the use of the loans and why in any one university loans can be granted, and yet, under exactly similar circumstances, a loan may be refused in another university.
Another matter which should be investigated is the present rate of taxation being charged settlers on small holdings under the Veterans Land Act. The intention of the act relating to small holdings, as originally drafted in 1942, was the settlement in semi-urban areas on a limited acreage with the opportunity to augment the small regular incomes. One of the main advantages was that of low taxes. The regulations set a ceiling of approximately $60; yet today we find that on some projects the settlers are having to pay taxes as high as from $150 to $270. There is a vast difference between $60 and $270. I have a brief on this question from settlers in the Bowness project, and I shall bring it before the committee when it is set up. If he has not already done so I hope that the minister will make a full investigation into the Bowness project to find if some form of relief cannot be given in that case. If it is not possible for the municipality to reduce the taxes, then I think there is some responsibility on the federal government to try to take care of the situation.
In closing I should like to say that some consideration should be given to the demands of the fire fighters in view of the fact that a definite promise was given to them upon enlistment that they would be considered in the same category as the men who served in the armed forces. We also feel that further consideration should be given to the merchant seamen. It is not necessary for me to refer to the wonderful record of these men to show that many of them served in far more

Veterans Affairs Committee
dangerous areas than many men who today are getting the full benefit of the veterans legislation.
Mr. HOWARD C. GREEN (Vancouver South): Mr. Speaker, in the course of the debate on the speech from the throne I spoke on February 19 about various aspects of veterans affairs, and I have no wish to cover the same ground today. However, there are three other points I should like to raise, and if the house will bear with me for a few minutes I shall try to make them clear.
In the first place, I urge that the minister and every member of the house accept the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and seconded by myself. As you will have noticed, Mr. Speaker, that amendment merely adds, after the words "His Majesty's armed forces", the further words "including the merchant navy". So that if the amendment is carried, the first paragraph of the resolution we are considering today will read:
That a select committee be appointed to consider the legislation relating to pensions, treatment and re-establishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces, including the merchant navy, and of other persons who have been otherwise engaged in pursuits closely related to war. and to make recommendations from time to time in respect thereto.
I suggest to hon. members that it will be of value to the committee if this resolution is adopted with the amendment included, because the committee may then take it that the merchant navy should be treated as the fourth arm of the services. During last session we had several debates on the question of whether or not the merchant navy men had received proper consideration; and personally I have been of the opinion, and I am today, that there is not a member in this house who does not believe that these men should be treated as though they had served in an arm of the forces. Therefore I suggest that we make it quite clear at this time by including the four words proposed.
I would refer hon. members to a promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on July 8 of last year, to be found at page 5210 of Hansard. He entered the debate on the question of whether the veterans preference in the civil service should be extended to men in the merchant navy, and he said:
.... the proper way to proceed would be to have the position of the merchant seamen further considered at another session of parliament. I will undertake to say that I would advocate that that course should Ve taken before a special committee in the light of what has been said here this afternoon.
If we go back to the speech from the throne in 1945 we find the following:
Our country will ever remember with pride the heroic exploits of Canada's fighting men and merchant seamen.
This implies that the government in 1945 considered that the merchant seamen were, in effect, the fourth arm of the services. I have here a magazine. Searchlight, published by men in the merchant marine, and it contains a statement by the Hon. Mr. Michaud. I notice the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) is smiling. There is a statement by him in the same publication, much to the same effect.

The minister has a pleasant smile and I am glad to see him smiling today. This is a statement by the Hon. J. E. Michaud, published in February, 1945:
No other body of men in Canada's fighting services has done more for the cause of freedom than those unsung heroes of the sea-the merchant seamen. All our war effort would be unavailing if it were not for the heroic devotion to duty of Canadian and other seamen of the allied nations. Merchant seamen virtually form the fourth arm of the fighting services.
There are statements to the same effect by several other ministers. In the proceedings of the veterans affairs committee of 1946 hon. members will find at page 41 this statement in a summary of evidence that had been taken by departmental officials in the recess between the two sessions. speechtext:
Mr. Randles stated that the percentage of casualties in the merchant marine was greater than in any of the other services, and I think that statement is correct.
The hon. member for Royal and myself suggest that this position be settled today by including the merchant navy as the fourth arm of the services. If the house sees fit to vote down that amendment, on the other hand, it means that those who vote against the amendment will be saying that the merchant navy was not actually the fourth arm of the services and. I think, they will be doing a great injustice to those brave men.
We found during the committee sittings of 1946 that the merchant seamen were falling
Veterans Affairs Committee

between two departments. They were, in the first place, the charge of the Department of Transport. Then, if they were to get adequate pensions and other benefits that were available for ex-service men, they had to get them from the Department of Veterans Affairs. I felt throughout the sittings that we were failing to give them proper consideration largely because they fell between the two departments. I suggest, therefore, that we make it absolutely clear that the committee is to see that they get justice in 1948.
There was also some objection by the government to including merchant seamen in the benefits, because we were told it would be hard to define just who should be considered merchant seamen, who should be entitled to get the benefits. I would point out that there is no longer any need to worry about that score, because we have here Bill G, passed by the senate this year, being an amendment to the Veterans Insurance Act, and in that bill we find a definition of merchant seamen which could be used in the other veterans legislation. That definition is:
(d) with a merchant seaman who received or was eligible to receive a bonus pursuant to the merchant seaman special bonus order, at any time within three years after the 31st day of August, 1946.
I do not think anyone can question that there has been and is today great unfairness to these men in the failure to give them consideration. I would point out to the minister that a merchant seaman cannot get a pension for a disability suffered or for a disease incurred unless that disability or that disease can be traced directly to enemy action. In other words, if he was disabled while at sea through the rolling of his ship, then he could get no compensation whatever; or if he contracted a tropical disease while in the tropics, or a disease in the orient, he could get no compensation. And, mind you, we have many such cases in Vancouver, because Vancouver is a great seaport. We have a great many men who served in the merchant navy. It is almost necessary for such a man to have been hit by enemy fire in order to qualify for the pension, and that certainly is a most unfair situation.
Then he cannot take training, he cannot get vocational training unless he trains for the sea. We had many thousands of men at sea during the war. In peacetime we have a comparatively small number. There is no chance for the great majority to go to sea again, and yet they cannot get vocational training unless they take it in connection with a seafaring life.

They cannot get educational benefits. The merchant seaman who may have been torpedoed two or three times sits at the same desk in university with the man who did not serve outside Canada. Yet the merchant seaman gets no help and the other lad does. I do not think anybody can suggest that is a fair procedure. Merchant seamen cannot take up a holding under the Veterans Land Act unless they happen to be pensioners, and there are only about thirty-two or thirty-three merchant seamen who are pensioners. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) can correct me on the figure, but I believe it is under fifty for the whole war period. They cannot qualify for a business or professional loan, and they do not get any preference in the civil service. I shall explain just how that happened. The committee were considering amendments to the Pension Act, and certain

Veterans Affairs Committee
amendments were accepted unanimously by that committee. One of them was an amendment haying to do with the matter of presumption with regard to pre-enlistment condition. I intend to deal with that further a little later on. Another amendment had to do with the deadline. In the Pension Act there is a deadline which provides that if a veteran of the first war marries after May 1, 1944, the wife cannot qualify for an allowance, and any children by that wife cannot qualify for an allowance. This special committee in 1946 brought in and adopted unanimously recommendations to deal with both of these situations. I have before me here a copy of the proceedings of that committee, if the hon. member for Rosthern has forgotten. But he was chairman of the committee, and I am quite sure he has not forgotten, because we had a considerable row about it at the time. After those recommendations had been accepted by the committee, government members were sent in to a meeting held three or four days later; we had come in government members who had taken no part, or very little, in the proceedings of the committee up to that time. There were several ministers there. Perhaps the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) was one of the reinforcements; parliamentary assistants were also brought in. A motion was moved wiping out those recommendations and substituting recommendations which the government wanted. This committee made certain recommendations, and I do not think that we can reverse those except by unanimous consent. By doing what you are doing now, I think you are reversing what this committee decided on.
I see no reason at all why this committee has to reach a unanimous viewpoint on every thing that is in this bill or why the government has to have a bill that is unanimously endorsed. We find, after every attempt to compromise, that we cannot reach something that is endorsed by everybody; and that simply means that on one or two minor things there is going to be some controversy in the house, when the government assumes the responsibility of bringing the bill down. I think that is their responsibility, and) I do not see why they do not take it.
Then farther down on the page he says:
But I am going to vote against it-
The amendment to which I was objecting, -because I do not think this committee can be forced by muscular strength to reverse something that they submitted and were prepared to vote on previously.
On the next page he said:
To me it is not a question of a legal mind at all. It is a question simply of-what will I say-a rough roller against people who are opposed to the views of the minister. I am
foing to support the minister in the house, but am not going to support the methods in this committee.
The hon. member for Rosthem subsequently raised a row about that statement, and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River withdrew it; but I have read from the record, and I do hope there will not be any back-tracking this time. You see, Mr. Speaker, those two points on which the government forced a change in the recommendations of the committee are still vital points. They are still unsettled, and they are still two of the most important points to be dealt with in connection with the veterans.
One has to do with the question of the preenlistment condition. Thousands of young Canadians have been refused pensions on the ground that they suffer from a pre-enlistment condition. Those young men were enlisted as fit. They were good enough to get into the army, the navy or the air force. A great many of them were good enough physically to be taken overseas. Now they are told by the commission that they cannot qualify for a disability pension because they are suffering 
from a pre-enlistment condition. We got the figures from the chairman of the pension commission in 1946. Then in 1947, when the estimates of the department were first up for consideration, I asked the then minister to bring his figures up to date, and he was kind enough to get them for me during the recess.
I have them here, up to June 30, 1947. These are the figures of the men who were taken into the forces as fit, who were discharged as unfit, yet who are refused any pension whatever, either for full disability or on an aggravation basis, on the ground that they were suffering from a pre-enlistment condition. Those who served in a theatre of actual war outside Canada numbered 13,321. Those with service wholly rendered in Canada numbered 72,340, or a total of 85,661.
You cannot tell me, Mr. Speaker, and you cannot tell any Canadian that this is a proper situation; that over 85,000 young Canadians should have been taken into the forces as fit and discharged as unfit, yet held not qualified for any pension whatever because they had pre-enlistment conditions. That is a situation which must be met. In the 1946 committee we tried to meet it by moving that thi3 presumption be written into the act:
There shall be a presumption that an applicant's condition as recorded on his acceptance as a member of the forces was in fact his condition at that time and that any subsequent deterioration during service was due to such service.
The idea was to put the onus on the state of showing that the deterioration in condition was not caused at all by service. I do not think the minister objected particularly, but the pension commission did not like it, and the matter was dealt with as I outlined' a few moments ago. The amendment may not be the proper way to meet the situation, but the figures speak for themselves. There is no reason why 85,000 Canadians should have to go through the rest of their lives disabled, after having been good enough physically to serve in the forces, without being able to get any compensation whatever for that disability.
The other point had to do with the deadline; and to mention it proves my case. . There is no reason why a veteran of the first war who married after May 1, 1944, should not receive an allowance for his wife and for any children by that wife. Those are two matters which must be straightened out by the committee this year.
My third point is this. I hope the powers of the committee will be deemed wide enough to permit it to bring in some recommendation for better treatment of the children of the men who died. Personally I believe the children of a veteran who died should be given

Veterans Affairs Committee
the advantage of vocational and university training at the expense of the state, just as their fathers would have had those benefits had they returned. At the present time the child of a veteran who was killed will not get that advantage, and as a result will be at a great disadvantage in life as compared with the child of the civilian or, for that matter, the child of the veteran who came back. So I suggest that the committee have power to recommend legislation to deal with this situation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, today the minister said he would like the amendments to the Pension Act rushed through the house, put through all stages. He did not make it clear whether or not he intended to refer that bill to the committee, but I suggest that going over these amendments would be one of the most important jobs the committee could do this session; that it rather makes a farce of having a committee if legislation of this kind is to be rushed through the house without first being referred to the committee for consideration. If the minister is able to do that with the Pension Act he will be able to do the same thing with the amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act; and when these two measures are out of the way the committee will be able to deal only with what is left over. That is not good1 enough.
The minister has not lived up to the statement he made on February 16 in regard to war veterans allowances. At page 1228 of Hansard he said:
The amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act are still under study, and the proposals will be completed before the end of the present week.
That was nearly three weeks ago, but since that time there has been no further statement. The only word we have had with respect to any improvement in the war veterans allowance legislation was the statement made by the Prime Minister on December 19; and what was promised then is entirely inadequate. I have no intention of repeating today what I said on February 19, but I do not think there is a member of this house, of any party, who believes that the proposed amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act are anything like adequate.
I suggest to the minister that the bill amending the Pension Act and the bill amending the War Veterans Allowance Act should go to the committee, not only in fairness to the committee but because then an opportunity will be afforded the Canadian Legion, the Army, Navy and Air Force, the Amputations Association, the Canadian corps, the Sir Arthur 5849-1251
Pearson club and the other soldier organizations to make their representations. The young lads from the universities, too, will have a chance to state their case. If these bills are not referred to that committee no such representations can be made, or if they are made they will have no effect. So I hope no attempt will be made to short-circuit the committee by putting this legislation through the house without having it referred to the committee. If that is done the importance of the work of the committee will be greatly reduced, and I think a great injustice will have been done to the young men and women who served Canada so well during the years of the last war, and also those older men and women who served during the first great war.
