I have served on two committees of this house on veterans affairs, and in my opinion the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) this afternoon made as good a speech as I have ever heard him make in this house. I thought it was factual, coming from one who has some knowledge of what he was talking about, and I considered it reasoned and fair. The fact of the matter is, he gave me the impression of being a very good lawyer judging from the way in which he assembled his facts, analysed them and put them before the house, and I think that, to any fair-minded jury, he would have won his case.
As regards this committee, I want to say that I, too, am sorry. I join with others who have stated that the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie who is now in the other place-and I hope he will be happy there-is missing. I know there is something missing on the other side of the house when I sit across here and see that his seat is occupied by someone else. I say, too, that I had a great deal to do with veterans legislation before ever I came to this house. I had the privilege of corresponding with the right hon. gentleman and of meeting him, and I always found him to be sympathetic and one who would do what he could within the confines of the legislation. That legislation will never be any broader than the treasury board wants to permit it to be. I know the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg), and I want to take this opportunity of saying that I am glad he is here in the post he now occupies. I know he will not go too far wrong in veterans affairs, because he received his early training on the executive council of the Canadian Legion in Nova Scotia. I had the honour of sitting there with him for a short time many years ago, when most of the legislation we are now talking about was in the embryo stage. I know he has watched it grow up from his place in this chamber, in the same way as most of us who are veterans in this house endeavoured to follow it as it developed.
I have no illusions about the committee. I do not believe in kidding myself or anyone else. I have a fairly good idea of what this committee will accomplish. It will accomplish exactly what the treasury board permits it to accomplish. The statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver South, when he says the committee is a creature of the government, is, I think, a fair statement. The com-

mittee cannot be anything else. When there is a majority over there on the other side, and the government decides to set up a committee for the purpose of analysing any problem, the majority of that committee will take directions from the treasury board in the matter of spending money. I say that every member- whether he was on the other side of the house or on this side-who sat on the veterans affairs committee or on the pension committee prior to it, was anxious to have things done regardless of party. I think the members took a fairly non-partisan attitude on these matters. But I know there comes a time when it is a matter of deciding on spending more money, and when the Minister of Veterans Affairs and his assistant must go to someone else who holds the purse-strings and say, "Can we get this money?" If the answer is "Yes," there is no difficulty; but if the answer is "No", then the government decide what is to be done, because they are in the majority on that committee; and the best that members can hope for is to try to provoke the thoughts of those who may have access to the treasury board, on matters affecting veterans on the outside with whom they do not come in contact every day.
I shall not repeat anything said by the hon. member for Vancouver South or by the h'on. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). That would be just a waste of time. I agree with the former in his analysis of this merchant marine question. I suggest that the amendment now offered should be adopted. At least it would guarantee that the terms of reference of the committee would be sufficiently broad to have the matter discussed by it. But if something like what is suggested by this amendment is not included, any discussion of the marine service in that committee will be precluded. At least, that is the way I see it. Apparently the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) does not see it in that way. But maybe when he consults the legal branch of some department, he will get another opinion as to what this means and he will say, "I am sorry; I did not think it meant that, but the legal branch tells us now that this is the correct interpretation, so that you cannot discuss the question". I think it is merely broadening the terms of reference to permit discussion to take place in the committee on that question.
There are two or three odds and ends that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and the hon. member for Rosthern with regard to veterans legislation. During the sitting of the last veterans affairs committee we had a great deal of discussion, and within the last couple of days I have re-read a great many of the recommendations which

Veterans Affairs Committee
were made on this matter of having our veterans legislation in this country reciprocal with veterans legislation in the United States, the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Australia. I think most of the bodies from the outside which represents veterans, and which presented briefs to us, brought in the suggestion that we should make our legislation reciprocal. The situation as it is now is causing hardship. For example, we have in Canada a few veterans who married widows overseas. They came back to Canada with their children, but because those children were not born in Canada they are not entitled to receive our family allowances, despite the fact that similar legislation is in effect in the United Kingdom.
I myself have run into several men who served six years in the British merchant marine. All during the time they served there they paid unemployment insurance to protect them against unemployment. At the end of six years they decided to come back to Canada. These boys land back in Canada; they cannot find a job, so they go with their card marked "paid up" a month or two weeks before leaving Britain, but they are told at the unemployment insurance office, "You are not entitled to unemployment insurance. We will see what we can do about a job". But this social legislation is not reciprocal with Britain, the Unites States or the other countries I mentioned.
These matters may seem to be trivial ones, but they are not to the individual who is affected. Whether only ten, fifteen or twenty men are affected, let us stop for a minute and think that every one of those people is a human being and he feels, just as much as you or I would, the injustice and the hardship that should be avoided. I generally try to place myself in their position. A man comes to me and says, "I did five years' service. A good deal of it was combat service in Italy and western Europe. But just toward the end of the war I went out one night and got into a little difficulty. I was sentenced to some time in detention." That man who was sentenced to detention lost his liberty. He lost his wages during the period he was incarcerated. But in addition to that, when he comes back to Canada he is further prosecuted by losing his gratuity. In addition to that, if he has a job- and I have run into several who were in this position-it lasted only long enough to make 107 or 110 contributions-I am actually giving the number of contributions-where it should have been 180 to the unemployment insurance office in order to qualify him for unemployment insurance. He is told, "You cannot qualify; you have not a benefit year estab-5849-126i
lished. But maybe we can get your armed service credits." This is where the soldier comes in. He is told, "If we can get your armed service credits, we can qualify you for unemployment insurance." So application is made for his armed service credits, and a note comes back to the effect, "Sorry; he cannot qualify for the simple reason that he got a misconduct discharge." I wonder how many of us ever stop to think for a minute of the kind of treatment meted out to a young man under those circumstances? In civil life you would not do that to him-take his pay from him, stigmatize him and deprive him of all social legislation. When you stop to think about it in terms of money alone, you will be surprised at the amount a young fellow like that loses. I think this is something which should be reconsidered and revised. I certainly think the armed service credits as applied to the ordinary service personnel in a matter of employment should be applicable in a case similar to the one I have set out here. Why should he lose everything just because he went out and had a few drinks of beer, and got into a little difficulty? I think most of us who were in the army could say, "There, but for the grace of God, go I." I believe that is the way we should look at it.
I am picking out these peculiar cases because, being a peculiar person, they come to me. I should like to bring another matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), which also has to do with the veterans. When I hear people talking about a committee, how we are to cure these problems in committee and all that kind of stuff, I think back to some of the things I have been talking about in the house for the last eight years. This is one of them. Away back in 1940 I ran into a case like this. While a veteran of the first war was overseas, his wife went to the United States and divorced him. He had nothing to do with it. He could not help himself; he was in the service. When he came back he found himself divorced. For pension purposes and all other matters of that kind that man cannot marry. If he does he commits bigamy, according to the decisions I have obtained, because we in Canada do not recognize a United States divorce.
I know of two cases of this kind. One man was issued a licence and married again. He was married for over twenty years, but he could never have his wife included for pension purposes. That was the case of a veteran of the first war. I have now another case of this kind from Ontario, and this man is affected in exactly the same way. He went overseas; his wife divorced him; he came back to Canada and found himself free, as he thought. He
Veterans Affairs Committee

-went out and obtained a marriage licence. I asked the late Hon. Mr. Lapointe when he was Minister of Justice, "If that man is not legally married in Canada why was he not prosecuted for bigamy?" No answer. "Why was he issued a marriage licence if he would not be entitled to marry?" No answer. "Do you consider it fair to keep a woman in that position for pension purposes, or for the protection of service personnel?" Well, he did not think it was fair; but the war was on; this divorce business was a rather touchy thing, and when we got this war off our hands we would consider that. At that time I was advised that a change would be required in the Canadian divorce law, but I do not think that is so.
I believe most of the things I am talking about here, the mean little things which set up a great deal of irritation, could be cured if the commission had sufficient administrative latitude. I have met quite a few of the people administering pension affairs. I think they are sane, reasonable and fair. If we would only write legislation flexible enough to allow them to make decisions in these borderline cases I believe a great deal of the trouble we are now having would be overcome, because it is in connection with matters of this kind that we are having most of our difficulties.
Another case is that of the young fellow who came back to his job on the railroad for a short time. Then the government said, "We will give you a course," so he took a course for ten months. When he finished there was no work for him. He applied for unemployment insurance. No unemployment insurance; he did not have sufficient contributions; and the ten months he spent taking a course, the cost paid by the government, could not be included for unemployment insurance purposes. That boy has been idle for over a year. He is still writing to me. Personally I think the ten months he spent in taking that course should be counted for unemployment insurance purposes. I do not see a reason in the world why it should not. So when the Minister of Veterans Affairs gets to know some of these things I hope he may be able to iron out some of the difficulties and knock off some of the corners.
I am not going to go beyond my time. I >vas rather provoked into getting up this afternoon by some of the discussion that took place. However, I would1 emphasize again this business of the merchant navy. I think a crying injustice has been done to the section of the service that fought the hardest battle of all. I do not think anyone equalled the hardships and misery the boys in the mer-

chant marine went through. There is only one thought I would leave with the hon. member for Vancouver East.-

They said, "We are responsible for your wages and your maintenance; we will see that any disability is taken care of," and so on. These were government-owned institutions, functioning under the direction of the Canadian government. The only section of the service that functioned under the system of free enterprise was the merchant marine. There we had private, separate companies, who received all the profits; but now that the war is over, they do not want to accept any responsibility. Mind you, I am not arguing against the boys in the merchant marine getting everything the people of Canada are prepared to give them through this institution of parliament. I am leaving this thought with the hon. member for Vancouver South, that you must get to the point where you are not only willing to give the government responsibility and authority but prepared to support them in connection with these institutions. A glaring example of the failure of free enterprise in fighting the last war was the treatment given the boys of the merchant marine after the war was over. No grateful company came forward to establish pension rights, hospitalization and all that sort of thing. That can be done only when the people of Canada give this government a mandate to go out and do these things, and to socialize the whole business all along the line. Then, and not until then, shall we eliminate injustice.

Mr. Speaker, three months after the opening of this session the new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) has introduced the following motion:
That a select committee be appointed to consider the legislation relating to pensions, treatment and re-establishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces and of other persons who have been otherwise engaged in pursuits closely related to war, and to make recommendations from time to time in respect thereto.
That the committee shall have power to send for persons, papers and records, and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee.
That the committee shall have leave to sit while the house is sitting.
That eighteen members of the committee shall constitute a quorum.
That the committee shall consist of Messrs. Baker-, Belzile, Benid'ickson, Bentley, Blair, Blanchette, Brooks, Oroll, Cruickshank,, Dickey, Dion, Emmerson, Gauthier (Portneuf), Gregg, Green, Harris (Grey-Bruce), Harkness, Her-ridge. Isnor, Jutras, Langlods, Lennard, Mac-
Naught, McKay, Marshall, Moore, Mutch, Pearkes, Quelch, Roes (Souris), Skey, Tucker, Viau, White (Hastings-Peterborough), Wright, and that paragraph 1 of standing order 65 be suspended in relation thereto.
May I, first take this opportunity to congratulate the new Minister of Veterans Affairs upon his appointment and to assure him that his comrades across this country will certainly look to him for real leadership. From his experience and his past association with the Canadian Legion I am sure that he is well qualified to look after the interests of the veteran, but I want to repeat what others have said that he will have to be prepared to battle with the treasury board if he wishes to put through certain recommendations which the committee may later on make.
I was pleased to hear the minister say that all matters relating to the Department of Veterans Affairs will be referred to the committee. I was a member of the veterans affairs committee which sat under the able chairmanship of Doctor Cyrus Macmillan, in 1942, and it was my privilege also to sit on the committee in 1946 under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). The committee of 1946 was composed of sixty members of the house, all veterans of one or two wars. Those members certainly put in long hours for many days and gave a great deal of thought to the veterans charter which was later introduced in the house.
In my opinion veterans legislation is never finished, and we might well have a standing committee of the House of Commons on veterans affairs. I wish to make some reference to this point at a later time. First, I wish to refer to the rather heated1 discussion carried on by the hon. member for Rosthern this afternoon on this topic. While he was going to be brief, he took his full forty minutes. He said he did not think the government were at all to blame because this legislation was introduced only at this time. My mind goes back to December 8 when we had a discussion in this house on procedure and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) introduced a resolution that government orders should have precedence after December 9. There was a heated discussion. I, along with other hon. members, at that time pointed out that I had many grievances which I wished to discuss on the speech from the throne, grievances having to do with veterans, agriculturists and others. After that discussion, a vote ensued in this house and we were defeated1 136 to 69. I am not sure that these are the exact figures. Then we debated the
Veterans Affairs Committee

throne speech periodically1 for a full three months, thr^e months last Friday, when I think it was disposed of.

speechtext:
I wish to occupy eight or ten minutes of the time of the house this evening to call attention to some features of this great problem of the care and treatment of returned soldiers from the last two wars. I wish to compliment the committee which has been acting in the last [DOT]two or three years on the fine charter it produced last session and the session before.
This committee has approached the important problem of returned men very largely from a non-partisan point of view and I hope that spirit will still pervade the committee. Once in a while there is a departure from it, but on the whole the committee has been non-partisan in its endeavours and I compliment them accordingly. I also wish to compliment the two Victoria Cross holders on this side of the house.
I should like to refer to certain features of the work of this committee, but before doing so I would point out that after the last war, when the soldiers were coming home after 1917, owing to the lack of hospital accommodation hundreds of young soldiers died from the flu in the camps in the Toronto district. There was considerable uneasiness

about that situation and we had an inquiry in a series of inquests at Toronto, as a result of which we discovered that there was an utter lack of hospitalization for the troops all over Canada. The result was that the government of Sir Robert Borden had to spend $35,000,000 in hospitals all over Canada.
The minister of militia, as he was then, the late General Mewburn, accompanied by me, looked at the Goodyear new building at Long Branch, but it was unsuitable and too far away, and it was decided to take the plant of the Kodak Company, called the Christie Street Hospital from then on. At that time the doctors were only on half or part time.
A great many improvements have been effected since that day. I may say that when I first brought up the matter of Sunnybrook hospital the proposal was unfavourably considered, Before that war I had been in communication with the owner of that property, the late patriot, Joseph Kilgour, urging him to devote it to civic purposes and in his will he gave it to the city for a park. After the last war broke out, I urged the city of Toronto in 1942 to make use of the site for hospital purposes. The late lieutenant governor, Hon. W. D. Ross, a splendid citizen; who died recently, was a warm friend of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and he offered several hundred acres of his large farm at Erindale on the Credit river free to the government. I thought it would be accepted. However, they later accepted Sunnybrook; I am glad they did at last get a wonderful hospital there; and improvements have been carried out which are of great importance. I hope Christie Street will in time be closed.
I believe there are some aspects of this problem of veterans that have not been considered. I refer particularly to the representations that have been submitted by the war amputations of Canada. This is an association every member of which has lost a limb, limbs or complete eyesight in fighting for Canada. In common with all other disabled groups they are seeking an increase in the basic rate on which compensation for their war disabilities is assessed, and they are asking for a level which will provide $100 per month for a 100 per cent war disability. The pension for total war disability has been $75 a month since 1921. It was fixed on the cost of unskilled labour in the general labour market of that time. The government proposes to increase it to $87 a month.
In twenty-seven years the improved standard of living in Canada has enforced large increases in income throughout all industry

Veterans Affairs Committee
and business. Advances of 40 per cent and more were widespread even before the recent meteoric rise in the cost of living. The increase offered the war blinded, war limbless, war paralysed and other war disabled would be regarded as most moderate. The industrially disabled draw workmen's compensation at current wage rates in their industries. By comparison the request of the war disabled is most modest. Yet they have made the greatest of all sacrifices for their country, short of giving their lives. They should be the last and not the first targets of government economy. That is correct, in my opinion. That is what they are asking for and I now most heartily' endorse the principle of $100 a month for a 100 per cent disabled fighting man. I hope something will be done along these lines by this committee.
I am glad to see that the work of the committee will embrace pensions, treatment and re-establishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces and other persons otherwise engaged in pursuits closely related to war, and that the committee will make recommendations from time to time in that respect. There is a strong committee from all sides of the house.
I will not go into all these matters, but I think the question of the blind and the amputation cases should receive very careful consideration. It is, as I say, a long overdue measure and further assistance should be given.
As regards the merchant marine, I was a former chairman of the harbour commission and one of the founders of the new harbour commission. I may say that I have seen these boys on ships on the lakes. I have seen the work they did before and during the war. I cannot speak too highly of the work done by the men of the merchant marine during the war. They went out to fight the battle of the Atlantic by night and by day, in the darkest hours of the war, when we thought the war was lost, in all seasons and in all climates. They stood by their ships, and many of them lost their lives. I hope something will be done for them this session.
I hope the committee will consider a further grant or bonus or subvention for the employees of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific railway and the other railways. A large percentage of them are returned soldiers. I think this bonus should be given for the way in which they transported the troops to the seaboard. Their work was most commendable, and they received nothing for it. In connection with demobilization, hundreds of trains ran to Halifax from all across the country. These employees have as yet received
nothing for their services from the corporations by which they are employed. I hope the committee will go into that particular feature.
Another matter I wish to mention is that of housing, which amounts to almost a scandal in this country'. I can tell you that, from what I have seen of these trailers from the train windows when coming into the city. I remember raising this matter in 1928 and 1929 with a former great newspaper man, Mr. Harry Anderson, editor of the Globe, who was one of the heads of the press gallery. He took it up in his paper. I do not know what would have happened to these returned men across the river if the wind had been the other way the night of the fire, two years ago, which nearly destroyed the bridge in Ottawa and even in some parts of this city where there are these trailers which should not be there. The returned men have a right to something better than things like that.
Then with regard to rent control, I know of no reason why a returned soldier should not be able to get into his own home. I have always urged that in the house. I know of some of these injustices. From what I have seen of these rental courts, the decision in many cases is far from being justice. I am surprised at the judges acting in them. I do not believe in the principle that judges should act in these particular courts.
I notice that in some of the law courts there have appeared some of these poor unfortunate soldiers in connection with income tax and petty violations of control regulations, who cannot make a living because of the high cost of living and so on. They are summoned before magistrates, county court judges and all that kind of thing. Some consideration should be given to these men. I hope that either the government or the soldiers' organizations provide counsel for them, because I see reports in many of the newspapers with regard to them. I have received as many letters as most hon. members, and probably more than some, from people who write to me from the Toronto district and other parts of the country. We need to have counsel for those soldiers who are brought before these courts. Something should be done about the high cost of living for them.
Then we have the imperials. There are thousands of these men in Canada. Some of them have been here since the last war and have been citizens for twenty-five years, and some of them do not get anything. I have known a great many of them, and1 some of their children and their children's children are suffering. The committee should include
Veterans Affairs Committee

them. Then there are the firemen. Some of these firemen have done splendid work overseas. I hope the committee will consider them. Then we see that some of the Hong Kong soldiers are not getting a real living allowance. I had a letter from a lady the other day who said her boy would never be the same. He is in hospital. As I see it, a great many of these troops should1 have been placed in the hospital or in a rest home for a year after they return home, because they will never be the same. I hope the committee will consider that feature and grant them equality of treatment with those who trained in the United' States.
I believe some direct federal aid should be given to the municipalities by way of direct aid toward relief, hospitalization and rest homes. I know a great many of these poor soldiers whose wives have to go out to work in the daytime, leaving their small children in rest homes for nursing, education and food. Some of these women work an eight-hour day. I hope some aid may be given to the municipalities for the half the cost in soldier cases and others. The burden should not be on the municipality for the treatment of these honourable patriots who suffered even unto death for this country in two wars and during the depression. I believe that some help should be given to them. I believe in the policy which has been urged in some parts of the country. I hope the committee will consider what should be done about these war memorials. After the last war a survey was made by the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) with regard to these after-the-war memorials-schools, community homes or centres, municipal institutions or something like that all over the country. I think the finest memorial you could build for the soldiers is to give them- proper and decent housing, increased cost of living allowances, and1 many of the other matters which I have mentioned.
There was a1 debate last session with regard to these war memorials. In our city the municipality paid for two or three of them.
I have forgotten just how many thousands of dollars, but there were some of them which the city pays for. I do not believe that the municipality should do so. There should be a national policy on all this relief. It should be national, not local, and1, if done, should be done by the federal authority. Otherwise we shall have the citizens of our cities paying for these war memorials in their own towns and for those in other parts of the country. I hope the committee will consider that.

Then there are the war students in our universities and colleges. When I see these magnificent institutions, Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment you on having a son attending the University of Toronto. He has been recently elected head of the students' council of one of the important colleges in that great university. We have 18,000 or 19,000 students in the University of Toronto. A large percentage of these men-over 10,000 of them- served in this war. I know a great many of
them.	I might mention Danforth Technical School, where the Governor General is to lay the cornerstone of a war memorial on May 30 next. I can tell you that there is a school that was used during the war, with 10,000, 11,000 or 12,000 students, by night and day. Great work was done in the secondary schools. I was talking to one commanding officer the other day, and he could not understand why the government did not give further assistance to the cadet services in secondary and other schools as formerly. The buildings have been provided, and the work of the cadet services is most commendable. These cadets will be needed in the years to come as soldiers and leaders of this country. While many of these soldiers now at the universities work in the summertime, many of them cannot get jobs
then.	I wish to commend the present minister for his interest in that branch of the work, war students at colleges. He himself was the head of a great university and I know he is interested in that particular branch of the work. I urge that it be further extended to all the universities of our country, with more liberal treatment in it.
Another matter which I should like to see the committee consider is that of positions in the civil service. I remember when I was head of the city we had a hard-and-fast rule that all assistance should be given to returned men, and that has been the universal rule in our city from the start, that they be given preference in all positions of employment.
I hope the committee will consider the matter of cadet service. I urge that, lastly, upon the minister, because he knows the value of cadet service to the people of this country. The cadets of today are the soldiers of tomorrow in case of another war in the future. We are not far away from war now, though by the grace of God we hope it may never come to this country again. We hope we may never be invaded, though we are pretty close to it now as in the last war. I urge that something should be done at this time for the cadet services to restore the grants and camps.
I am sorry the Minister of National Defence

Veterans Affairs Committee
(Mr. Claxton) is not here tonight. I think he made a fatal mistake last year when he eliminated the cadet services from his program. In all wars, from the South African war and long before, to the two great wars, the cadet services have been the backbone of our militia, as they are today. Ask any commanding officer where his men come from; he will tell you that what I say is correct.
I do not know that I can add much more, except to say that I do not like all these evictions of returned men which are taking place throughout the country. They are a disgrace to Canada; and it is also disgraceful that soldiers cannot get possession of their own homes. I do not know where we are heading in regard to these matters, and I hope attention will be paid to them.
I want to compliment the various members of the committee. They did noble work in years gone by, and I hope they will get together this year and bring these matters up to date, so that the returned men will urge their sons and others to enlist if trouble should again come. If trouble does come on land, sea or in the air, as it may, I hope the committee will recommend the re-establishment of the air training program for the whole empire, as a defence measure for the empire. That should have been continued; we should never have let it drop.
Having offered the committee these few suggestions, I hope they will get to work soon and that the report they bring in will be a blessing not only to the people of this country at large but especially to the returned men and their wives and families.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not like the impression to get abroad as a result of this debate that the people of Canada have in any way changed their attitude toward our veterans. The people of Canada are just as enthusiastic today about showing great generosity and gratitude to those who served overseas as they were at the conclusion of either the first or the second great war. Nor would I like the impression to get abroad that the returned men feel that the people of Canada have not shown gratitude for their services. I believe the majority of the veterans feel that their sacrifices have been well recognized by the people, and they are grateful for all that has been done to enable them to become re-established in civilian life. They are also grateful to their comrades who are serving as officials in the Department of Veterans Affairs, whether on the pension commission, on the war veterans' allowances board, on the boards
in connection with rehabilitation or in connection with the Veterans Land Act. Veterans are serving in all those capacities; and the ordinary run-of-mine veteran in the country appreciates that they are trying to give him a square deal. Of course they realize that these officials are circumscribed by the laws and regulations which have been laid down, and that it is not within their province to go beyond those regulations. But I believe the officials of the department have endeavoured to interpret the laws as generously and sympathetically as possible.
I am proud to have been nominated as one of the members of this committee. It has not been my privilege to serve on committees for a number of years, though I did have the pleasure of serving on the committees of 1945 and 1946. This afternoon some reference was made to the activities of the 1946 committee, and perhaps I might give the impressions of a newcomer as -to how that committee functioned. During the first months of its sittings I was surprised at the non-partisan attitude adopted. Various briefs were presented by the different veteran organizations. They were listened to attentively; comments were made, and it did not matter which party a member of the committee might represent in this house, he tried to deal with the problems as they were presented to him and to give -the opinion of a veteran trying to work out the best possible scheme for his fellow veterans. But as time wore on and it became necessary to reach a decision in certain matters, one noticed a considerable change. New faces appeared at those meetings, and I remember so well the hidden legions being led forward by a minister of the crown, now the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and overruling the recommendations made by the impartial members of the committee in earlier sessions. During a previous session of this parliament I referred to the mobile reserves which were brought up. I have a vivid recollection of those mobile reserves moving in, not unlike the Hun divisions which moved in after the first battle of Cambrai.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PENSIONS, TREATMENT AND RE-ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I had not the wit to coin the phrase uttered this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), who referred to that committee as a creature of the government; but I did come away from the later sessions of that committee with the firm conviction that we had been made tools of the government.
Veterans Affairs Committee

I am pleased that this new committee is being set up. I hope it will not be placed in a strait-jacket as was the previous committee of which I speak. I appreciate the remarks of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg), who says he will welcome suggestions as to how improvements may be made in veterans legislation. For fear some restrictions may be placed on the committee, I should like to take a few minutes this evening to offer one or two suggestions to which I hope the committee will be able to give consideration. I seize the opportunity to speak to the members of the committee now, and I hope this will enable them later on to give full consideration to what I am about to suggest.
Referring, first of all, to the amendment which has been proposed, I am heartily in favour of introducing into this motion now the fact that the committee must consider the merchant navy. If those words are included in the motion the committee will be obligated to consider the services rendered by those men. Again I recall what happened in the 1946 committee. Several hon. members suggested at that time that we should give full consideration to the benefits which should accrue to the members of our merchant marine. There was some rather desultory discussion of the part that the merchant navy had played in the general scheme of winning the war; there was some rather happy-go-lucky discussion of the type of benefits that they should receive, but when it came down to making a final decision the merchant navy was jockeyed out of position. There was a suggestion that their benefits should be considered in a separate bill, that they should not be included in the Pension Act or the War Veterans Allowance Act or other benefits which affected the armed services. Therefore I am anxious to see this committee charged with the responsibility of making a recommendation to the government as to exactly what benefits the men of Canada's merchant navy should receive.
There was some mention this afternoon about the merchant navy and the armed services. Do hon. members realize that the members of the merchant service were armed, that they had quick-firing guns on their vessels in order that they might deal with any hostile submarine? Do hon. members know that they regularly kept watch with their anti-aircraft guns so that they might engage any hostile aircraft which might fly over their vessel? I hope hon. members on all sides of the house will support the recommendation to include consideration of the benefits which should come to the men of the merchant marine and charge the committee with giving careful consideration to them.

I was pleased to hear the Minister of Veterans Affairs announce, when speaking about pensions, that the cheques for the increa'ses were already prepared and that he hoped to get them out for Easter. My query is: Why wait until Easter, midsummer or next Christmas? Let us get them out now. Why not send out these cheques tomorrow? When they are sent out I hope he will say that it is only in part payment because, if this committee gets the opportunity of hearing the recommendations of the various veterans organizations, there is no doubt in my mind that it will come forward with a recommendation to increase the increases of pension which the government has already recommended. I say, let it be made quite clear that these additional cheques are merely part payment of what I hope will be an additional increase to be approved when the committee has made its recommendations based upon the briefs which I hope it will listen to from the various veterans organizations.
I am not going to labour the point because twice this session I have pleaded for additional increases for the veterans. I remember an old saying: There's luck in odd numbers, says Rory O'More. Therefore I do not hesitate in saying for the third time, almost on St. Patrick's day: let us have additional increases to these pensions in view of the present increases that are recommended being totally inadequate.
The same thing applies to the war veterans allowances. I have spoken about this before and suggested that the regulations with regard to the amount a veteran may earn and still receive an allowance be simplified. But above all things I urge that the increase be made automatic in order that we do not have to refer back to the board to see whether a man already granted an allowance because he was needy can prove that he is still needy or perhaps more needy in order to obtain an. additional allowance. I urge also that the war veterans allowance be extended to cover more persons.
I would suggest, first of all, that the committee give careful consideration to allowing members of the Canadian expeditionary force of world war I who, through no fault of their own, got only as far as Great Britain, who were held there for various duties and were not granted the privilege of serving on the continent of Europe, to come under this legislation. It seems to me that those Canadians of that original expeditionary force should be granted the same benefits as those now granted to Canadians who served only in Great Britain in world war II. It should be

Veterans Affairs Committee
remembered that there were more casualties in Great Britain.' through meningitis on Salisbury Plain during world war I than there were from German bombings. It may be that this phase has been overlooked, but the records show more casualties on account of exposure on Salisbury Plain than from bombings.
When considering the extension of war veterans allowances to veterans of world war I who served only in Great Britain, let us remember that Canadians who served in the northwest field force, commonly known as the Riel rebellion, men who served only in Canada, are entitled to these allowances. Surely men who crossed the Atlantic and were exposed to submarine attacks during the first world war are just as much entitled to consideration as veterans who served only in Canada in the northwest field force.
I should like to refer to those veterans who served with British forces other than those of Canada, commonly known as imperials. I would put them in two classes. First, there is the man who was domiciled in Canada perhaps for a number of years before the outbreak of the war. Perhaps for business reasons, perhaps to complete his education or for some other reason he went over to the United Kingdom a short time before the war broke out in 1914. These men were anxious to serve their country and, giving no consideration to what unit they joined, they joined up with the first regiment accepting recruits. The first contingent of the Canadian expeditionary force did not arrive until some time after, so that these men joined up with any regiment which was mobilizing. Then, after the war, after they had served with the imperial forces, they returned to Canada. Those men are Canadians. They may have been bom1 in Canada; they may have come to Canada from the old land two or three years before. I received a letter this very morning from a man who came to this country in 1905, remained here until 1912, then went over to the old country for business reasons and joined up immediately on the outbreak of war. When the first world war was over, he returned to Canada. He is a Canadian in every sense of the word but he is deprived of the benefits of the war veterans allowance. I can see no reason why that class of imperial should not be included in the benefits of the war veterans allowance.
Others are those men who served in an actual theatre of war and, after service in the first world war, emigrated to Canada, and here in Canada they lived for perhaps twenty years. Personally I believe they also should be included in the benefits of the war veterans
allowance, and that they should also have the benefit of our Canadian hospitals. The next point I want to make, and I hope that this will be taken up in the committee, is that there should be a new definition of "western hemisphere" as applied to the War Service Grants Act. I should like to see the definition extended so that those men of the 34th company of the Veterans Guard of Canada who did their duty in British Guiana should have an opportunity of receiving the benefits under the act. Those men volunteered for active service wherever they might be, and they were sent, not to Europe, but through a submarine infested Caribbean sea down to South America, where they had strenuous and dangerous duty to perform. There they were separated from their families for two or more years. Owing to a narrow interpretation which is given to the term "western hemisphere", they are deprived of the benefits of the act. I feel that they should be given an opportunity to have their case considered. In the previous committee they submitted a brief; but on November 25, 1946, the chairman of the committee advised the author of the brief that it could not be considered during that session of parliament owing to the amount of work before the committee. I hope that now, after the lapse of all these months, the chairman will allow the original brief as submitted by the representatives of the 34th company of the Veterans Guard of Canada to be considered, with a view to seeing whether they are not entitled to some benefits in recognition of their service in British Guiana.
Some references have already been made to the members of the ferry command. They were Canadian, British and United States pilots who flew some 11,000 aircraft from Canada to the various theatres of war. They actually landed in North Africa only a short distance behind the troops, who were engaged in battle. There they delivered their aircraft, and they delivered ammunition and supplies. It is a matter of record that three out of every four of the pilots of the ferry command lost their lives.
I should like to put forward a special plea for the widows of the Canadian members of the ferry command. In British Columbia I know of some widows of pilots of the ferry command who are in very much straitened circumstances. I know of one case where there are three orphan children who have to depend entirely upon charity for their livelihood. They receive no pension; they receive no gratuities. Yet at the same time the British government has quite recently given full recognition to the members of all civilian aircrew and considers them on a par with service
Veterans Affairs Committee

personnel in so far as benefits and service decorations are concerned. I hope that the minister will charge the committee to give this class full consideration and to call evidence in order to substantiate my claim that the men of the ferry command should receive greater consideration, and particularly that their widows and orphans should have more generous treatment accorded to them.
I have one more point which I am not quite certain will come within the province of the committee, but I would ask that the question be reviewed by the committee. I speak of those veterans who were serving in the permanent forces of Canada and who took their discharge under what is known as part V of the militia pension scheme. They were regular sailors, soldiers or airmen who had expected to complete their service agreement of twenty or more years before they drew their pension. Owing to circumstances connected with the war, they found that after fifteen years of service, and sometimes less, they were given an opportunity to retire under what is known as part V of the militia pension scheme. They were given the opportunity but actually they had very little choice in the matter, because if they had remained on they would have had to take a very much lower rank. In many cases it was considered advisable, and rightly so, to stream-line our forces, and men who had reached middle age were not required in the armed forces of the country in peacetime. The point that is causing this type of veteran considerable hardship is that he is prohibited from enjoying the full benefits of his pension scheme if he accepts employment in the public service of Canada. When they joined up ten or fifteen years ago they realized that that was a condition of the militia pension scheme, but they also realized that by the time they had completed their service they would be getting on in years and would be drawing a larger pension than the one they now draw under part V of the Militia Pension Act. But they are handicapped now because, if they accept employment in the public service, they cannot receive the full benefits of the Militia Pension Act, to which fund they had contributed during the period of their service.	.
The public service of Canada has expanded considerably. It is no longer merely the civil service, but all these crown companies which are springing up to take care of various industries are considered as part of the public service of Canada. I suggest to you, sir, that a man who has spent a number of years in the armed service of the country is by virtue of his training, his adherence to discipline and punctuality, which has been instilled

into him, particularly suited in many cases to service in these crown companies or in the public service of Canada; and I would ask that the committee's scope be extended to give consideration to the advisability of modifying those restrictions in some way so as not to discourage this particularly desirable type of man.
I have covered a good many points. The minister asked for suggestions. I have tried to give some suggestions which I hope will be of benefit in guiding the committee's deliberations. I hope that the committee will be set up without further delay and will be able to get down to work, and that, after its deliberations and it has heard the evidence which will be placed before it by the different bodies which are to appear, when it has made its recommendations the government will pay heed to them.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PENSIONS, TREATMENT AND RE-ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish briefly to express concurrence in the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) to set up a select committee of the House of Commons to consider the legislation relating to pensions, treatment and reestablishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces, and so on. It seems to me that this debate should have been the opportunity for those of us who this year are not to be favoured by being on the committee itself to pass on through you, Mr. Speaker, and through the Minister of Veterans Affairs, to the committee some of the points that arise in our minds as to what should be the scope of the activity of the committee when it starts to function.
I wish to refer for a moment to the amendment that was introduced this afternoon in the name of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). With respect to that portion of the resolution relating to pensions, treatment and re-establishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces and of other persons who have been otherwise engaged in pursuits closely related to war, the hon. member for Royal brought in an amendment specifically mentioning the merchant marine. He emphasized that some consideration should be given to the merchant marine. I believe that all hon. members are concerned that the merchant marine should be properly re-established, as should be the members of the armed forces.
However, this occurs to me in connection with the amendment, and I want to ask some of the legal minds in the house a question on this matter. At the moment there comes to

Veterans Affairs Committee
my mind the contribution made by some of the fire fighters or of the personnel of the Red Cross or of the members of the ferry command or of the various other auxiliary services which are not at the moment recognized for re-establishment on the same basis as that of those who wore His Majesty's uniform. It seems to my non-legal mind that the fourth line of this resolution would have made complete provision for a discussion at least of further measures of rehabilitation for those groups which I mentioned, which are exclusive of the merchant marine. I do not know just why the hon. member for Royal considered the merchant marine as worthy of singling out at this stage. I want to pay them every tribute, but I recall the excellent work of the fire fighters overseas, and it would seem to me that they should be placed in this group as well. To my mind the resolution as it stands is sufficiently inclusive. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether you would permit me to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) at this stage, or perhaps he can answer it after I sit down if he prefers, just to what extent the reading of the resolution as it stands on the order paper would exclude, or otherwise to what extent the groups I have mentioned come within the scope of the resolution without applying the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Royal. To my mind the thing is redundant; but not being trained in legal matters, it seems to me that the wording is perfectly clear to include all these groups that I am interested in, as well as the fire fighters. I would appreciate it if the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who has some training in these matters, would express an opinion as to the comprehensiveness of the scope of this resolution with respect to the group that I have mentioned other than the merchant marine. Then, of course, in his capacity as leader of the house at the moment he could assure us whether or not we would be excluded or whether the committee would be excluded from discussing the various matters relating to their re-establishment as they are brought up. I should like the minister to make a note of that as well.

If we do that then, of course, we shall have to include the fire fighters and those other groups who saw service in an actual theatre of war, as most of us are aware. However, I shall wait until the minister makes a statement in that regard if he will be so kind.
My purpose in rising was to offer a suggestion or two. I want to concur in the argument of those hon. members who have suggested that this committee be a standing committee of the house and that it do not just sit when the Minister of Veterans Affairs has some special thorny problems to place before it.
For quite a number of years yet we shall have to have continuous changes in administration and legislation covering re-establishment matters, and I would favour this committee being a standing committee of the house. I think, too, that the committee should be asked to consider pensions, treatment and re-establishment as specified in the resolution, but it seems to me that there is a broader aspect of this whole matter which they should consider. I believe there is a basic relationship to the special needs of discharged persons which should be considered-veterans of the war and war casualties and their families. These should be considered specifically as such; but as we get farther away from the war, then I think there should be some sort of co-ordination between the consideration given the needs of veterans and their families, having regard to the peculiar nature of war disabilities and the results of the war, and the needs of the citizens generally from the point of view of social service. That is to say, if there is, by virtue of public opinion at the present time, need to consider these matters, then it should be done as I suggest. If such a condition occurs that veterans rehabilitation, pensions, treatment, allowances and so on are given a certain emphasis in relation to our budget, and at the same time old age pensions, family allowances and the like are allowed to remain as they now are, and if there is no co-ordination or no relation between the two, then eventually we shall think of this as class legislation rather than as re-establishment legislation. The time is coming soon when there should be a co-ordination between veterans' matters and matters of social welfare affecting the basic needs of Canadian citizens generally, and legislation on the two aspects should be
Veterans Affairs Committee

dove-tailed in some respects, paying special regard, of course, to the peculiar needs of war veterans themselves and their families.
There is something else in connection with these allowances that are prescribed by statute. We fix these allowances periodically, every twenty, twenty-five or thirty years, or after sufficient public opinion has been built up for the purpose, and there is little actual relationship between war veterans allowances and pensions for war casualties, and the actual purchasing value of the money which they receive by statute. Our economy in the last year particularly has been so vulnerable to outside influences, or to government policy, that the cost of living has risen at a terrific speed, and there is no way in which compensation can be given to these people who have no earning powers so that they may have a living as adequate in 1948 or 1949 as they had on the same monthly cheque in 1946 and 1947.
I submit that the time has come to set basic pensions and basic treatment allowances, and then the government should in effect give bonuses automatically, based on the changes and fluctuations in the cost of living which are in large measure due to the policies of the Canadian government and for which, therefore, the Canadian government must assume full responsibility specifically.
I believe we all favour in this house increased allowances to student veterans and to pensioners; but simply to say, let us increase these allowances by ten., twenty-five or forty per cent is not a solution. It is not a cure for the straitened circumstances in which a person may find himself in consequence of the cost of living having fluctuated this way or that. In my opinion it would be much better to set these pensions at a base figure once and for all and then supplement them according to the fluctuations in the cost of living index, paying the difference as a supplement.
I would like the committee to consider an extension of the housing program so far as veterans are concerned. Unless a veteran and his family are able to take advantage of the Veterans Land Act and settle on a farm or a small holding, and that includes only a small portion of the number of men and women who have been in uniform, there is no opportunity to secure much needed1 housing. Some members may say, "Well, we have a wartime housing scheme by which the veteran may be able to rent a home." That is true for some if they are so fortunately situated1 that they may qualify for houses under Wartime Housing. Or, you may say, if he has money let him buy a home under the integrated housing

plan. To my mind, that scheme for veterans is a distinct and utter flop. I recall specifically the case of a young man in my own city who purchased1 under the integrated housing scheme, or thought he was purchasing, a four-room house for $6,060, and when the time came that the contractor had completed the house this veteran found that, unless he was to take a chance on the down payment he had made to the construction company, he had to put up another $1,300 additional payment in order to get possession of a four-roomed house, or $7,300 for a small dwelling of that kind. It is utterly fantastic. The contractor was protected in his cost by the National Housing Act, but the man whom we thought we were protecting took the rap again by paying on an already inflated price another $1,300 before he could secure possession of his house.
I suggest that the committee should make a strong recommendation to the government this time that the housing schemes of the country be so enlarged that veterans might use their re-establishment credits to take advantage of alternative types of housing to that provided by the Veterans Land Act so that they can settle in urban areas, if they wish to do so, having the same right to receive grants from the federal purse as those who are fortunate enough to be settled under the Veterans Land Act.
Other groups could be included in this housing re-establishment as well as those in uniform, and I refer to the groups I mentioned earlier in my talk.
There is one other thing the committee should consider. I have spoken to a number of civil servants who enlisted at the beginning of the war, whose superannuation rights on enlistment were automatically suspended at that time and who now find, five or six or seven years after they enlisted, that they have to start all over again to build up superannuation credits. Surely that is very shabby treatment for the federal government to give its own employees when they are re-established.
I feel that the veterans affairs committee should see that our own federal government be as generous as they have expected private concerns to be in the matter of taking back returned men.
I wish the veterans affairs committee every success in their deliberations if and when the committee is set up, and I hope it will be set up early.
I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will rise when I sit down and give to this house some assurance that it is not necessary to have the Tory amendment voted on at this time. Perhaps the Tories will withdraw it.

Veterans Affairs Committee

As I see it, the wording of this resolution seems quite satisfactory to me, but I should like to have a definite government assurance on that point.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): The hon. member asked for a definite assurance that the resolution as drawn covers and was intended to cover all those for whom there are already legislative provisions relating to pensions, treatment and re-establishment. That is quite clear. The question was specially considered by the government when the terms of the resolution to be put on the order paper were being approved. There are a large number of persons other than members of the armed forces for whom there have already been made legislative provisions relating to pensions, treatment and re-establishment. For instance, there are the merchant seamen and salt-water fishermen; there are the auxiliary services including several branches determined in the statute. There is the corps of civilian fire fighters for service in the United Kingdom; there are the R.C.M.P. special constables. The air raid precaution workers are included. Under part VIII, there are the voluntary aid services; that is, the Red Cross and the St. John Ambulance workers. Under Part IX, there are the overseas welfare workers; under part X, the Canadian civilian air crew of the R.A.F.. commonly called the ferry command. It also includes veterans of the allied forces who are not members of His Majesty's armed forces. It includes the Wrens, the South African military nursing services, the special operators, and there may be others. The government wished to have the terms such that all those who could possibly come within the description of having been engaged in pursuits closely related to the war could bring their grievances, if any, before this committee.

I do not altogether agree, Mr. Speaker, with your statement that it does not add anything to the resolution. As a matter of fact, I do not think the government would be so much concerned if it did not add anything to it. Our object has simply been to place the merchant marine in a position which the government themselves have repeatedly stated they should be placed in; that is, that they were one of the four fighting services of this country. The minister speaks about placing them in the same category as the Red Cross workers, V.A.D. workers, fire fighters and so on. We recognize that these people all performed splendid services. But when we recall that the men of the merchant navy had more casualties than had any other branch of the service-and that has been definitely stated in this house

and that the suffering that these men had to endure was as great as that of those in any other braneh of the service, we in the committee felt that these men-

Yes, and their dependents. Many of these men died. They died by the hundreds. In our veterans affairs committee, time and time again members from the other side of the house as well as members from this side felt that these men should be included as one of the fighting branches of the

service. Our amendment, Mr. Speaker, is simply to have these men included as one of the fighting services. The amendment would have the resolution read:
That a select committee be appointed to consider the legislation relating to pensions, treatment and re-establishment of former members of His Majesty's armed forces, including the merchant navy.
Some hon. members have confused this with the next section, which speaks of "other persons who have been otherwise engaged'' and so on. We know that will include the merchant marine; we know it will include all the other people the minister has mentioned, but we want the merchant marine included in a different way. We want them included as one of the fighting forces, and that is the reason for our amendment.

Mr. Speaker, this delightful, remarkable example of co-operation between the C.C.F. and the government rather reminds us of old times, with such carefully framed questions giving rise to such carefully framed answers. The amendment of the official opposition having been ruled out of order, the subject matter before the house is now the resolution proposed by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg). Before I go on with my remarks in that regard, I should like to refer to the implication sought to be left this afternoon by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Tucker) that if we take much time in discussing this resolution, and particularly if we ask that the amendments to the Pension Act be sent to the veterans affairs committee, we shall be guilty of obstruction and delay. I would point out that the only time effective action can be taken to increase pensions and veterans allowances this session is when the legislation is before the house; and the best way to get amendments to the government's present proposals is to have those proposals sent to the veterans affairs committee, where they can be discussed and the pros and cons debated. Them, after the various matters are considered in the impartial and constructive manner we hope that will be done, if it can be shown that further increases are justified those increases will be made.
If, on the other hand, we allow the legislation to go through this house virtually without
Veterans Affairs Committee

protest, as we are being invited to do, simply in order to avoid the charge of obstruction and delay, then we shall have lost our chance of actually obtaining increases under the present proposals. It is an old tactic to put poor legislation or inadequate legislation or undesirable proposals before an assembly and then, when objection is taken and it is suggested that the legislation could be improved, to charge the opponents with obstruction, and try to ram it through on that basis. It is a tactic we saw operated time and again under constitutions and types of government we thought were different from our own. That is a tactic which I think should be deplored in this house, especially when it is used in connection with veterans legislation.
