I have to confess that that was not my understanding of the hon. member's remarks this afternoon and I am glad he has cleared up that point for us. I hope, then, that the government will accede to the request which has been made that the proposed pensions legislation be sent to the veterans affairs committee.
In considering the subject matter of the resolution before us, I think it would be useful to go back to the statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the beginning of the session and again on February 16 with regard to the proposed legislation concerning veterans affairs. On December 19, before Christmas, the Prime Minister opened his statement in the house with the following words, 'to be found on page 489 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, the government has for some time been giving careful consideration to the nates of pay of members of the civil service and the armed forces, and the rates of veterans pensions and war veterans 'allowances. I,t was recognized that account should be taken of increases in the general level of wages and salaries since the establishment of the existing rates.
I would direct attention particularly to that sentence to the effect that account should be taken of the increases in the general level of 
wages and salaries. The Prime Minister having made that statement, I think it was to be expected that increases in veterans benefits would actually bear a relation to that other level. But having said that, the Prime Minister announced increases of 110 a month in the case of a 100 per cent pensioner, or 13-3 per cent. I shall give the figures in a moment which show that the increase in the genera! level of wages has been in the neighbourhood of 65 to 70 per cent. As the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) said immediately, it was a tragic and terrible let-down.
Then the Prime Minister made a statement on February 16, in which he admitted that representations had been received from all veteran bodies and that, partly as a result of those representations, further careful consideration had been given to the matter. He went on to add that the legislation was practically completed and he tabled details of the increases to be given. The wording of that statement created the impression of generous treatment, but no specific figures were given at the time. Figures were tabled only.
An examination of the tabled figures shows that the first impression of generous treatment was completely misleading. The increase announced on December 19 was 13-3 per cent for a 100 per cent pension, and the increase announced on February 16 brought it up to 16 per cent for a 100 per cent pension. Certain of the percentages given in the table produced at the time created an erroneous impression, particularly the percentage of increase in the case of married student veterans. The increases to which I shall refer are to be found in the table placed on Hansard, but I am reading now from sessional paper 131F of the same day, Monday, February 16,
1948.
From those figures we find that a widow with children used to get $97; she now gets $114, which is an increase of 17-5 per cent. A 100 per cent pensioner with children gets the same increase, 17-5 per cent. It is represented in the table that in the case of student veterans, taking university or vocational training, the increases range up to 50 per cent, but the only justification for that figure is that the allowance is broken down into various categories. Instead of taking the married student and his wife together, the increase for the wife is-listed separately and that is shown as an increase of 50 per cent from $20 to $30. When the increases to the student and his wife are taken together they represent an increase of only 12J per cent. It seems to me that when you are dealing with allowances to married

Veterans Affairs Committee
veterans the only basis that should be used is the family unit. If all the increases given are added together it is found that the average increase for a veteran, wife and children is about 18 per cent. The effective figures for the increases in veterans benefits under this legislation vary between 16 per cent and approximately 20 per cent.
I have obtained Department of Labour statistics showing the increases in the wage rate. I should like to bring again to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the fact that the Prime Minister stated that in a consideration of this matter effect should be given to the general increases in wage rate. If we take the general index for wages as given by the Department of Labour, with a base of 100 for 1939, we find that ,n 1925 it was 93-8, increasing to 155-2 in 1946, or 61-4 per cent. I am told that during 1947 there has been approximately a 10 per cent additional increase. I am starting with 1925 because that is the year in which the basic rates for pension were established.
Similarly if we take the index for unskilled labour, which I understand was the one used when the scale of pensions was set in 1925, still taking a base of 100 as of 1939, we find that it increased from 92-4 in 1925 to 165-9 in 1946, or a total of 73-5 per cent. Wages have gone up an average of 70 per cent, while the increase in pensions over 1925, even on the most generous estimate, is approximately 20 per cent.
It seems to me that this is another case of letting down the veteran. Some of us feel strongly about this, more strongly than the words we are inclined to use. In my first speech in this house I referred to the matter of letting down the armed forces, and I said I would not refer to it again unless I felt that history was repeating itself and that the lessons of the past were being neglected. I feel that that is taking place. We have the government saying to the veterans that they will give increases which will bear relation to the increases in the general wage rates, but we find that when their action is actually analysed it does not carry out their words, because their words would entitle the veteran to an increase of at least 50 per cent, and their actions give him an average increase of less than 20 per cent. So we see history repeating itself, and we want this matter sent to the veterans affairs committee and the government to suit its action to its word and give the veterans the treatment they deserve.
I want to read an open letter addressed to the Prime Minister from one of the legion
branches in my constituency, because it puts the situation in apt and well chosen words. It was an open letter, a copy of which was sent to myself; it appeared in the press, and therefore it may be read to the house. It is dated January 21 and was written before the second announcement of increases on February 16, but the increases covered by this announcement represented only some three per cent, and therefore I have no hesitation in saying that the words in this letter are as applicable after the announcement as they were before. The letter reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
The members of the branch and all veterans of the district wish to take this opportunity to vigorously protest the manner in which your government is conducting veterans legislation.
At the last special session of the house your government refused to give priority to the business of veterans legislation on the grounds that it was not an urgent matter. This action is beyond all comprehension to us in view of the ever-soaring cost of living even by government index, which is not anywhere near accurate. The failure of your government to increase veterans pensions and widows allowances immediately, is causing extreme hardship and privation.
In order to refresh the memory of your government it is necessary to digress somewhat at this point. Only a few short years ago when the shadow of the swastika threatened to darken the entire civilized world, nearly a million young men and women, without thought for their own private future or safety, without benefit of contract or negotiation, interrupted their lives to take up arms for freedom and democracy. Mr. Prime Minister, the plight in which we find our veterans, their widows and dependents today is not the democracy thousands fought and died for. And until these injustices are remedied we shall not consider the last battle as being over.
With great dismay we now read in the press of your proposed increases in pension rates and widows allowances, which are not only inadequate but insulting. It will do little or nothing to alleviate the suffering of veterans, their widows and children. It will do nothing but prolong their privation and humiliation because their fathers gave their lives for their country. It will do nothing to inspire them to greater things which should be their right. Nor will it, Mr. Prime Minister, gird them to combat the otheT menace which is again threatening our country from without and within-the hammer and sickle.
In conclusion, Mr. Prime Minister, we wish to repeat that us a veterans organization we shall continue to fight with every rightful means at our disposal until such time as these cruel injustices are rectified.
Yours very truly,
Ashcroft Branch No. 113.
Canadian Legion, B.E.S.L.
That is a sentiment expressed in words which I consider it a privilege and am proud to support.
Veterans Affairs Committee

With respect particularly to the pension and disability benefits to be paid to our war veterans, there are certain suggestions which I should like at this stage to put before the house so that they might in turn go before the committee. I would also request the minister to be kind enough ,to make some reference to this matter in closing the debate. I have not dreamed up these recommendations myself. They are the result of what careful study I have been able to give to the matter in consultation with veterans organizations. They are an attempt to arrive at a reasonable statement of the opinions of experts whom I have been able to consult.
The first recommendation is that there should be a change in the terminology in the Pension Act from war disability pension to war disability compensation. The reason for that may seem to be a technical one; but it is urged, and I believe there is good ground for it, that by the use of the wordl "pension" employers 'are apt to come to the conclusion: This man has a pension; therefore I need give him only a lower paid job. Or when the employer is dispensing with the services of some of his employees he may dispense with the employee who has a disability pension rather than someone who has not a pension; whereas if it were put on the basis of disability compensation the question of the amount of the man's compensation for war disability does not and could not be allowed to enter the question of his wages or salary on receiving employment. On that point I object strongly to a statement made in the magazine issued by the Department of Veterans Affairs itself. In its issue of March 1, 1948, there is an article dealing with "The Disability Preference in Civil Service of Canada", and the article shows just how far astray our attitude to pensions and the effect of pensions has gone. In the article I find this sentence:
Needless to say the amount of pension awarded is intended to be significant of the candidate's remaining capacity for work.
It seems to me that this sentence reflects the attitude that a pension is a reward1 for inability to work, based on the loss of the man's earning capacity in the labour market. I am going to suggest that that is a wrong approach, and it is very unfortunate that it should1 have been allowed to creep into an article in a magazine published by the department itself.
In considering the approach which I think should be placed before the committee in a review of pensions legislation, I would suggest the following: Those who are interested in pensions and veterans affairs generally will agree that the proper basis, and the basis on

which I understand the matter was first placed, is that since the war service of the veteran has resulted in disablement, the country owes him compensation in so far as it can make up for the disability he now suffers. Therefore the degree of disability and the degree of pension awarded must bear a real relationship and what must be considered1 is the actual disability, plus the amount of pain and suffering, plus any psychological as well as physiological handicaps suffered by the veteran. We must attempt to assess the man's disability as a percentage of total disability, not how much less he can earn in the labour market. How much has he lost by his wound? In that way we can assess the percentage of disability.
Then we come to the basic rate of compensation, the money value of the compensation, and that is where the difficulty arises. For that possibly some yardstick must be used, but that rate must surely bear a real relationship to present-day standards. The rate must, as the Prime Minister said, take into account the increase in the general rate of wages. The rate must be the measure of compensation which the country wishes to pay for the disability the veteran has suffered, and surely the country does not wish to pay niggardly compensation but wants to be generous and to have the compensation bear a real relationship to current wage and salary levels. If that is the case, and surely there can be no doubt of it, the demand of the various veterans' associations that the rate for 100 per cent disability should be increased to $100 a month is only reasonable, and is perhaps even underestimating what should be granted.
I suggest, further, that, as in the case of the disability compensation, it must bear a reasonable relationship to present-day standards, so also must widows' compensation and so also must war veterans allowances. In that connection I should like to support what has been said on so many occasions with respect to the extension of the benefits of the War Veterans Allowance Act to imperial veterans. These are now Canadian citizens. They fought in the same war. There is no reason why, after fifteen years' residence in Canada, they should not be entitled to the same benefits.
I should like to suggest that there should be laid before the committee for its consideration the case of the helpless and the introduction of amendments designed to bring the helplessness allowance more into line with the requirements of present-day conditions. I refer particularly to paraplegics and quadra-plegics and other totally disabled veterans. Some of them are now in receipt of a helplessness allowance, the maximum of which is $750 a year. That sounds like quite a lot,

Veterans Affairs Committee
until you consider that these helplessly disabled and totally disabled-I am speaking in terms of physical disability, not in terms of earning capacity-have to hire a taxi every time they go downtown. They must pay an extra tip to somebody to put their wheel chair in the back of the car, close the door, and take them out again. Every time they need a haircut or wish to go to a movie they have additional expense, the extent of which is almost beyond our comprehension until we sit down and calculate it with pencil and paper. Besides their possible extra suffering, their psychological suffering, they have expenses all the time. Particularly if 'they are married we find that what actually happens under the present rate of helplessness allowance is that their wives become their attendants. I am quite certain that no government would ever permit that condition to continue if it were forcibly brought to their attention. The government never intended that the wife should become the 100 per cent full-time attendant of those helpless veterans.
While I am on this subject, I wish to deal briefly with remarks that are frequently made that, while there are some criticisms which might be made of the scale of veterans benefits, still Canada is far and away ahead of anything in any other country. That is not altogether correct, and particularly it is not correct in connection with the matter of helplessness allowances. In New Zealand, for instance-I am basing these figures on a comparative study in the last section of the "veterans charter"-one finds that the helpless allowance is $1,040 a year if it is necessary for the veteran to have an attendant. That is based oh the pound at $4. In the United States an attendant is provided; a conveyance is provided free of charge, and pensions up to $3,000 a year may be paid in special cases of disability. Therefore in Canada I suggest that, in the case of helplessness, the 100 per cent allowance should be increased to not less than $100 a month, because if your basic compensation rate is designed to compensate for the degree of a man's disability, bis physical and psychological disability and physical and psychological suffering, then, however generous you are in setting your compensation for that suffering, that compensation can only take care of the general case, and the special case of those totally blinded, totally or partly paralysed, double amputees or those in any other ways rendered totally or partly helpless requiring special attention, must be taken care of by an additional and generous helplessness allowance.
These are some of the suggestions that should be placed before the committee. Others 5849-127
would have to do with the case of student veterans, particularly the married student veterans whose increase is only 12J per cent. There are many things which I should like to say; but in view of the lateness of the hour and the anxiety to conclude tonight, I shall just refer to them in passing. It is well to remember that in the United States, in New Zealand and in Australia student veterans are in receipt of one or both of travelling allowance and an allowance for books. Our student veterans tell me that, in the case of single veterans, if they could receive the book allowance it would help greatly to tide them over the difficulty. As for the married men it cannot be denied that the increase of only 12^ per cent is not an adequate increase in view of the increase in the cost of living and in the general scale of wage rates.
In closing I should like to summarize the matters that I think should be laid before the committee for its consideration. They are as follows: first, a change in the terminology to that of war disability compensation instead of disability pension; second, an increase in the basic rate for 100 per cent disability to at least $100 a month; third, an increase in the rate for total helplessness allowance to at least $100 a month, and in the degrees of helplessness should be included such things as blindness, double amputations as well as para and quadraplegics; a further increase to take care of student veterans; and such other matters as have been previously mentioned, for instance the Veterans Land Act and the veterans living in wartime houses. I would ask the minister if he would do us the courtesy of referring, at least in passing, to these matters before closing the debate.
Mr. L. W. SIvEY (Trinity): Mr. Speaker, before I commence my remarks I just wish to say that some of .the problems which have been presented in the last five and a half hours have been indeed staggering and show clearly how badly the House of Commons needed to discuss these matters.
At the outset, may I offer briefly my congratulations to the minister on his maiden speech in the house and at the same time to pay my personal tribute to his painstaking assistants in D.V.A. who have performed their duties so conscientiously so far as their mandate permits. May I also say, regardless of party, that I am one who appreciated in full the energy and application of the former minister and his great service to the war veterans of Canada. I appreciated the irn-
Veterans Affairs Committee

mediate action which always was taken on the problems sent to him by veterans and other members of the house.
There is no need for me to refer to the fact that this committee and this resolution should have been called earlier. That has been ably dealt with by my colleagues. The few minutes that I shall take can certainly not delay the setting up of this committee and the veterans benefits which I hope will accrue from it. When the government finished the work of the 1946 committee it had not completed its job. The committee had gone as far as it was permitted to go, and it is my belief that it should have been permitted to meet again in 1947. However, in 1948 we find the situation doubly aggravated, not so much by what the government would not permit us to do in 1946, but more so by the government's financial policy which has resulted in inflation and rising prices. On top of this financial policy followed the embargoes which caused further scarcity with still higher prices. All these things have their tremendous effect on (pensions, allowances, benefits and dependents allowances. Those living on them have been affected most grievously. It is not now a case of the cost of living with these people; it is a case of the cost of keeping alive, and those on fixed incomes, as every member of this house knows, are without protection against this tremendous rise in prices.
Let me briefly cite some of the people who have written to me, to show the uniformity of their complaints. The Native Sons of Canada have written calling attention to the effects of the rising cost of living and have also described Canada's pension debt as a debt of honour to the veterans. The war amputations' association has also written. L will say no more, but I endorse the remarks of my hon. friend, the member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), with regard to their just case. I have had two letters from Christie Street hospital calling attention to the housing difficulties of veterans and the tremendous rise in the cost of living and the difficulties it has brought about. I have received a signed letter on how to starve on $30 a month and a budget is laid out therein. I have had an unsigned letter from a homeless widow showing her dire plight, with the rising cost of living and the difficult housing situation. From the Victoria College Union I have received a letter calling attention to the severe financial difficulties of both single and married students. The ex-service committee of students administrative council of the national council of student veterans have written to call attention to the same thing and

to point out how their education is being jeopardized. Branch No. 455 of the Canadian Legion at the University of Toronto has also stated the same thing. I have a full brief from the national council of veterans' association in Canada covering the whole situation and making recommendations. There can be no doubt that their brief and the Canadian Legion's recommendations should be endorsed. All veterans' organizations should be called on now to send their briefs to Ottawa so that otxr committee may arrange for their priority in appearance before it.
There are certain other immediate considerations which have to do in one instance with hospital allowances. If you can imagine a veteran in a hospital receiving $10 a month for incidental expenses, it is not necessary for me to describe the hardships he suffers, unable to buy even the smallest of personal comforts with this very meagre amount of money.
Then there is the length of time which pension appeals take. This in my opinion should be drastically reduced, and with it we should also consider the stabilization of the world war pensions at fixed levels after they have been paid for a certain fixed period of time.
Student veterans have also asked for a uniform interpretation of the students loan legislation across Canada. They ask that loans be underwritten by the Department of Veterans Affairs; that special loans be granted to those whose benefits have expired, and also that there be a student representative on the board,
I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that these are all reasonable requests. The single student veteran is in no less a plight than the married veteran, and he or she requires the same or the equivalent of any additional allowance that may be granted to married veterans. In many cases they have courses which require their full time. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the science courses require long hours of laboratory work and they have, of course, their other long hours of additional study.
I should like briefly to endorse what has been said by many others on this side of the house concerning both pensions and allowances, concerning merchant seamen, the means test for veterans allowances, the operation of the Veterans Land Act, a permanent veterans committee, ferry command veterans, fire fighters, war amputations cases and the many other classes of veterans or near veterans to whom the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) called attention a few moments ago, including the R.C.M.P. special constables, A.R.P. workers, St. John

Veterans Affairs Committee
Ambulance, overseas welfare organizations, veterans of allied forces, Wrens, South African nurses and many others.
But there are two cases which I particularly wish to refer to, and they are, first, the case of the Red Cross overseas veterans. The Red Cross, as you know, goes on into the peace. It is an organization that never stops. These girls who went overseas, in many cases at considerable cost to themselves, have received no benefits at all for their great service in world war II, and I feel that benefits for them should be given special consideration by our committee.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has already called attention to the second case I want to mention, which is that of the Hong Kong veterans who have been denied the Pacific pay which they, above all others, so justly earned. I consider it scandalous that they have not received the allowances due to them.
I close within the time limit which the minister asked, by saying I hope that we can meet immediately this resolution is passed and that we can agree to the wide reforms which are necessary. I hope that we shall operate swiftly in the interest of our fellow-Canadian ex-service men.

speechtext:
I do not wish to delay the passage of the resolution and I will take just one minute on behalf of the many veterans and veterans' organizations in Calgary that have asked me to take part in the debate. I should like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that the feeling there was universal that the increases announced by the government were completely inadequate.
The veterans and their organizations in Calgary consider that the disability pensions, the pensions to widows and the war veterans allowance must be increased. The veterans' organizations there are particularly concerned over the situation of the older veterans, their difficulty in getting employment, the level of war veterans allowance, and the allowance under that act to dual war service men.
I should like particularly to ask the minister to give consideration to these men. In the coming years they will be the ones who will need and must have increased pensions if they are to get by. All the veterans with whom I have spoken at home have looked for great things from this committee, and I trust that the committee will not disappoint them and that the implementing of the committee's recommendations by the government will be forthcoming rapidly.
Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I should like to say, first of all, how much I appreciate the fact that members of the house have made it possible to look forward to having this committee set up before adjournment tonight. I know hon. members will not expect me to cover the many points raised this afternoon and evening. It would be unfair to attempt to do so. I assure hon. members, however, that I have listened carefully, and the record of Hansard will be studied and the points brought forward will be submitted to the committee.
In one or two cases I was requested to deal with some particular matter tonight. The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) brought up certain points. I have already studied them, because they have been represented to me by veterans' organizations, and since these matters, I anticipate, will come before the committee, I think it would be wrong for me to deal with them at this late hour.
There is one point, however, with which I should like to deal, and that is the matter as to whether the bill for the increase in pensions, which is No. 18 on the order paper, should or will come before this select committee. If this resolution passes now, Mr. Speaker, and I stop talking soon, it is my intention to ask for the unanimous consent of the house to move No. 18 up one or two stages so that it may perhaps come forward to the select committee during the next day or two. That is the answer to that question. I shall be glad to have this bill come before the committee on veterans affairs if it can be so arranged.
I do not intend to add any more, except one point which five or six speakers mentioned, and that was regarding veteran students. I should like to make this point, that the recent increase was an increase to help married students take care of their families. The federal scholarship, namely, the tuition which is what it costs to pay the bill at the university and the living allowance for the veteran as a veteran was not changed. The tuition was whatever the university charged the veteran student, plus $60 a month, and so it remains. The increase was to assist in taking care of wife, children, mother and father if the veteran has them as dependents. I just wanted to make that point clear.	,
Motion (Mr. Gregg) agreed to.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REFUSAL TO PAY BENEFITS TO PERSONS RECEIVING VACATION PAY
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Can he inform the house if the unemployment insurance commission is refusing to pay unemployment insurance benefits to persons who receive annual vacation pay at time of termination of employment until the period covered by the vacation pay has expired? If this is the case, can the minister tell the house under what authority it is done?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: REFUSAL TO PAY BENEFITS TO PERSONS RECEIVING VACATION PAY
speechtext:
The unemployment insurance commission does refuse to pay any unemployment insurance benefits to a person while he or she is on retirement leave with pay. Authority for that is given by section 29 (1) (a) of the Unemployment Insurance Act which reads as follows:
29. (I) An insured person, shall be deemed not to be unemployed
(a) during any period for which notwithstanding that his employment has terminated, he continues to receive
(i) remuneration . . .
It has come to my attention that in some instances civil servants retire with six months full pay and allowances. The view taken by

The Address-Mr. Fulton
the commission, and I think it is a sound one, is that actually they, are receiving their full remuneration during that period and are not unemployed within the terms of the act.
The other point raised by my hon. friend is this. In many provinces in Canada, certain stipulated vacations with pay are allowed by law, and some by trade union agreements. I agree with the commission that, where a person is receiving full pay for holidays under the law or by agreement with the employer, within the terms of the act he is employed and is not entitled to benefits under the scheme. Then, of course, there is the over-riding factor that all have the right to appeal to a board of referees in whatever district they belong, this board being composed of an impartial chairman, representatives of the trade unions or workers and the employers' organization. I hope that is the answer my hon. friend wanted.

subtopic: REFUSAL TO PAY BENEFITS TO PERSONS RECEIVING VACATION PAY
speechtext: I wish to ask a supplementary question andi I should like the minister to look into this matter a little further. A person is not supposed to be working when he is receiving vacation pay. Would the minister try to ascertain how it can be assumed that he is either on retirement pay or that this is in lieu of any other remuneration that he could receive? This is vacation pay, and he is not supposed1 to be working when he is getting his vacation pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: REFUSAL TO PAY BENEFITS TO PERSONS RECEIVING VACATION PAY
speechtext: I will answer that immediately. I think, when a person is receiving full pay for holidays, he does not come within the terms of the act. I think that is sound and reasonable. To say that he should is, I think, stretching it a little bit too far.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My understanding of the situation, Mr. Speaker, is that the various amendments have now been disposed of and that the house is now considering the address itself. In the few moments that remain at my disposal tonight I should like to revert to a suggestion made in all seriousness during the course of the debate, to which as yet the ministry has made no reply nor has it given any indication of its attitude. I refer to the suggestion that there should be an immediate statement on the part of Canada as to her foreign policy, particularly with respect to recent and current events in Europe. I refer also to the request made by members on this side, particularly the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) and the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), for a debate on foreign affairs. There has not been a reply either to the suggestion made in the course of the throne speech debate or to the request made on the orders of the day; nor has there been any indication as to the attitude of the government. Since we think this matter is so important; since we think it is one of the most important questions facing the coutry and the world at the moment, we consider it essential to take this opportunity to introduce a discussion of foreign affairs.
If it is the wish of the house I can continue until eleven o'clock; but, if not, I would
The Address-Mr. Fulton

appreciate it if I might be allowed to call it eleven o'clock and move the adjournment of the debate.
